title: Adding Your First Data Source
content: A hands-on walkthrough of connecting Amperity to a brand's first data source, covering the shared courier pattern behind Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and SFTP, then contrasting it with Amperity Bridge for Snowflake's bidirectional, zero-copy connection built on Snowflake Secure Data Sharing.

sections.heading: Connections and the Quick Start Workflow
sections.body:
Before Amperity can resolve identities or build customer profiles, it needs a connection to wherever a brand's data actually lives. A connection points Amperity at one external location — an Amazon S3 bucket, an Azure Blob Storage container, a Snowflake warehouse, a Databricks lakehouse, a Google BigQuery dataset, or a standalone SFTP site. Amperity supports all six out of the box, and you set them up from the Identity resolution page inside Quick start, Amperity's guided setup area for connecting sources and preparing them for identity resolution. From there, an Add data source dropdown lists all six types.

Selecting most of these types — Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, or SFTP — opens a dialog literally titled Add courier. A courier is Amperity's internal name for one configured pull job: a specific file, or a filename pattern matching a family of files, on a specific external server, checked on whatever schedule you choose. Every S3, Azure Blob, or SFTP source you add is a courier, even though the term rarely shows up outside that dialog title.

Snowflake is the exception. Choosing it opens a different, purpose-built configuration flow instead of the courier dialog, because a Snowflake connection isn't a file pull at all — it's a live data share. That distinction, covered later in this course, is the biggest fork in the setup experience: everything else you add behaves like a courier; Snowflake behaves like a standing bridge between two systems.

sections.heading: The Pull Pattern Shared by S3, Azure Blob, and SFTP
sections.body:
Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and SFTP all funnel through the same five-step courier pattern, just pointed at different protocols. First, credentials: a courier can't be created until a credential for that storage system already exists in Amperity, so you pick one from a dropdown and click Continue. A 'Connection successful' status confirms Amperity can actually reach the location before you go any further.

Second, you name the source and tell Amperity which file to pull, either by browsing the storage system directly or by supplying a filename pattern for recurring loads whose names vary slightly — a datestamp appended to an otherwise identical filename is the typical case. If this is a brand-new source, whichever file you pick becomes the schema sample: Amperity reads its structure and uses that structure as the expected shape for every future load. If the source already exists, the file you select for this load has to match that previously defined schema, or the load won't proceed cleanly.

Third, encrypted files get a PGP credential field so Amperity can decrypt them before reading. Fourth, you review the file's inferred formatting — delimiter, compression, escape character, quote character, and whether the first row is a header — in table or raw view, and correct anything Amperity guessed wrong. Fifth, you pick a load date that falls after the file landed in storage but before today, and click Run.

Supported formats span CSV, JSON, Parquet, DSV, and others; deeply nested or complex JSON and XML sometimes need a separate 'legacy courier' configuration instead of this flow. One hard limit worth knowing up front: a PGP-encrypted Parquet file has to be under 500 MB to be previewed in the dialog before you run the load — it can still load past that size, you just can't preview it first.

sections.heading: Snowflake: A Bidirectional Bridge, Not a File Pull
sections.body:
Amperity Bridge for Snowflake works on a completely different mechanism than a courier. It relies on Snowflake's own Secure Data Sharing feature — a Snowflake platform capability that lets two Snowflake accounts read the same underlying data through Snowflake's services layer and metadata store, without either side copying files or scheduling an ETL job. Because of that, the integration is explicitly bi-directional: data can move both from Snowflake into Amperity and, unlike a courier, back out again, without a nightly file drop in either direction.

Setting it up starts the same way — Snowflake from the Add data source dropdown — but the dialog that opens asks for organization name, account name, and region instead of a credential dropdown. The region value comes straight from Snowflake's own CURRENT_REGION() function, run in a Snowflake worksheet. Next you supply a secure share identifier to establish the connection itself, then choose any combination of schemas and tables to bring in. Selecting a whole schema pulls in every table currently in it, but a table added to that schema later doesn't appear automatically — you have to add it by hand.

The last step is mapping each selected table to an Amperity domain table — Amperity's standardized internal shape for a category of data, like transactions or loyalty activity, that every other Amperity feature reads the same way regardless of which source it came from. Mapping in this dialog does not, by itself, assign a primary key or apply semantic tags to the table — those are separate steps (covered in the next course) unless you build a custom domain table, which lets you do primary keys and tags in the same pass. Saving and syncing kicks off the actual data movement from Snowflake into Amperity.

A few constraints are specific to Snowflake: field names have to be entirely uppercase or entirely lowercase — mixed case is flagged as unsupported — and a handful of Snowflake types (FILE, GEOGRAPHY, GEOMETRY, VARIANT, VECTOR) aren't supported at all, while semi-structured ARRAY, OBJECT, and MAP values need a defined, fully structured schema before they can share.

sections.heading: SFTP: The Simple, One-Way Counterpart
sections.body:
Where Snowflake is a live, bidirectional share, SFTP sits at the opposite end of the spectrum: it's explicitly pull-based and unidirectional. Amperity always initiates the connection and retrieves files from the SFTP server; the server has no way to push data to Amperity, and Amperity never writes anything back to it. If Snowflake is a standing bridge, an SFTP courier is closer to a scheduled visit — Amperity shows up, takes what matches the configured file or pattern, and leaves.

The setup steps are the identical five-step courier pattern from the previous section: select an existing credential and confirm 'Connection successful,' name the source and point it at a file or filename pattern, set a PGP credential if the file is encrypted, review the inferred delimiter/compression/escape/quote/header settings, then pick a load date and click Run. The documentation even uses nearly the same language for the credential requirement as it does for S3 and Azure Blob — 'credentials allow Amperity to connect to SFTP and must exist before a courier can be configured to pull data' — which underscores that this isn't a different mechanism wearing a different name, it's the same courier mechanism pointed at a different transport protocol.

SFTP tends to be the right fit when a partner or vendor already has an automated export landing on a server on their end, and you just need Amperity to come get it on a schedule — no cloud storage account or data warehouse required on either side.

sections.heading: Choosing a Connection for Your Situation
sections.body:
Which connection type to add first comes down to where the data already lives. If a brand's customer data already sits in Snowflake, the Bridge is the natural choice: no load dates to manage, no scheduled pulls, and updates on either side stay in sync through Secure Data Sharing rather than a periodic file drop. If the data instead arrives as files — a vendor's nightly export, an internal analytics bucket, a partner's SFTP drop — Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and SFTP all behave identically once you're inside the Add courier dialog, differing mainly in which protocol they speak to reach the file.

For a first connection, it's worth prioritizing whichever source holds the most identity-bearing personal information — names, emails, phone numbers, physical addresses — since that's the data identity resolution actually needs to start linking records together. The next course covers how to tell Amperity which fields in that source count as a primary key and which values should be excluded before any of it feeds into identity resolution.

quiz.question: What makes Amperity's Snowflake integration fundamentally different from its S3 or SFTP connections?
options: It uses Snowflake's Secure Data Sharing to exchange data through Snowflake's own services layer, giving bi-directional access without copying files.
It uses Snowflake's Secure Data Sharing to exchange data through a scheduled nightly export job, giving one-directional access without copying files.
It skips the credentials step entirely, connecting directly through a public Snowflake account with no authentication required at all.
It only supports loading a single named table per connection, unlike S3 or SFTP couriers which can load entire folders unattended.

quiz.question: In the S3, Azure Blob, and SFTP setup flow, what happens to the first file you select for a brand-new data source?
options: It is discarded after the connection test, and a blank schema is created for you to fill in by hand.
It is converted immediately to Parquet format, regardless of its original file type or encoding.
It becomes the schema sample that defines the structure future loads for that source must match.
It is sent to your Amperity account team for manual review before the courier can be activated.

quiz.question: Why does SFTP count as a simpler connection than the Snowflake bridge, according to the setup docs?
options: SFTP requires no credentials at all, while Snowflake requires an organization, account, and region to connect.
SFTP is a pull-based, one-way courier, while Snowflake is a live, bi-directional data share.
SFTP automatically applies semantic tags on load, while Snowflake requires every tag to be set by hand manually.
SFTP supports unlimited file sizes for preview, while Snowflake limits every table to 500 MB total in size.

title: Primary Keys, Exclusions, and Clean Input
content: Covers how to choose a stable, unique primary key so Stitch can recognize returning customers instead of creating duplicates, and how to exclude bad values, dates, and rows before they reach identity resolution.

sections.heading: What a Primary Key Is and Why Stitch Needs One
sections.body:
A primary key is a stable, unique identifier for the rows in one source table — the field Amperity uses to recognize that a given row belongs to a specific real person, load after load. It's the anchor that connects source data to Amperity's own concept of identity, called an Amperity ID: the single identifier Amperity assigns once it has determined that records from one or more sources describe the same person. That matching work is performed by Stitch, Amperity's identity-resolution process, which compares records across sources and decides which ones belong together; a primary key is what lets Stitch recognize an incoming record as an update to someone it already knows, rather than mistaking it for a brand-new person.

Without a reliable primary key, that recognition breaks down in a very concrete way. If a customer updates their phone number or shipping address, Amperity needs to treat that as an edit to an existing profile — not the arrival of a new person who happens to share a first name with someone else. A source table with no stable, unique identifier gives Stitch nothing to anchor that recognition to, and updates risk either fragmenting one person's history across multiple Amperity IDs or, in the worst case, merging two different people's data because a placeholder value briefly looked like a match.

sections.heading: Two Qualities of a Good Key: Unique and Stable
sections.body:
A usable primary key needs exactly two properties: uniqueness, meaning its value distinguishes one row from every other row in the table, and stability, meaning that value doesn't change over time for the same record. Both are required — a field can fail on either one independently. 'first_name' is a poor choice because it isn't unique: plenty of customers share a first name. 'updated_at' is a poor choice for the opposite reason — it's often unique at any given moment, but its value changes every time the record is edited, so it fails stability. A field like 'customer_id' pulled from a point-of-sale system is the strong example: it uniquely identifies a customer and stays fixed no matter how many times their other details change.

That pairing shows up concretely downstream in the Unified Coalesced table, where every record is identified by combining its source (the datasource) with its primary key value — and each such datasource-plus-key pair links to exactly one Amperity ID. A weak primary key doesn't just cause abstract confusion; it directly produces bad pairings in that table.

You don't have to pick primary keys by inspecting every column yourself. From the Identity resolution quick-start screen, the AmpAI Assistant — Amperity's built-in AI helper — can automatically recommend a primary key (and applicable semantic tags, covered in the next course) for each table. Alternatively, you can configure both manually if you already know which field qualifies.

sections.heading: Excluding Values, Dates, and Whole Rows
sections.body:
Primary keys control which rows Stitch can reliably track; exclusions control what Stitch is allowed to see in the first place. Amperity supports three kinds of exclusion, all reachable from the Data exclusions card on the Identity resolution page: specific values, which get converted to NULL wherever they appear; specific date values, entered in YYYY-MM-DD format through the NULL date values section; and entire rows, matched against criteria you define in the Row exclusions tab.

Configuring any of these means choosing 'Manually select' or 'Edit' on that card. Values you exclude are matched case-insensitively, and you add them by typing a value and pressing ENTER or RETURN — there's no separate save step. One formatting quirk worth knowing: special characters like an ampersand have to be wrapped in both parentheses and single quotes, written as '&', for Amperity to treat them as the literal value rather than as syntax.

sections.heading: Why Clean Input Matters Before Stitch Runs
sections.body:
Separate from anything you configure manually, Amperity applies one exclusion-adjacent behavior automatically: every field that has a semantic tag applied gets trimmed of leading and trailing spaces before it's used further. That's not optional and doesn't require a Data exclusions entry — it just happens as part of tagging.

Manual exclusions exist for the cases automatic trimming can't catch: placeholder values like 'N/A' or 'unknown' typed into a field, obviously-fake test records, or dates that represent 'no data' rather than a real event. Left in place, those values don't just clutter a profile — they can actively cause false matches, since two unrelated customers who both have 'N/A' sitting in the same field can look, to Stitch, like a shared identifier.

Both primary key selection and data exclusions happen on the Identity resolution quick-start page, before Stitch ever runs against the data. That ordering matters: they're preparation, not cleanup applied after the fact. A well-chosen primary key tells Stitch which rows to track as the same person over time; a clean set of exclusions makes sure the values Stitch is comparing are real customer data and not placeholders masquerading as it.

quiz.question: Why is 'updated_at' a poor choice of primary key for a source table, according to Amperity's guidance?
options: It only accepts numeric values, and most Amperity source tables use string identifiers instead.
It is not present in most source systems at all, so Stitch is never able to read it as a field.
It uniquely identifies a row but takes up more storage space than a shorter customer_id field.
Its value changes whenever the record is edited, so it fails the stability a good key needs.

quiz.question: Which of these three types of data exclusion does Amperity's Identity resolution page actually support?
options: Specific values, individual dates in YYYY-MM-DD format, and entire rows matching defined criteria.
Specific values, entire columns grouped by data type, and any row that contains a null field somewhere.
Specific tables, individual users identified by Amperity ID, and any column tagged as PII data.
Specific values, entire schemas grouped by source name, and rows older than a set retention date.

quiz.question: What happens automatically to fields that have a semantic tag applied, without any manual exclusion step?
options: They are converted to uppercase so semantic matching stays case-insensitive across every source.
They are copied straight into the Merged Customers table, bypassing the Stitch process entirely.
Leading and trailing spaces are trimmed from the field's values before further processing occurs.
They are flagged for manual review by the AmpAI Assistant before any load is allowed to complete.

title: Tagging Data with Semantics & Finding PII
content: Explains how semantic tags standardize customer-profile fields across differently-named source columns so Stitch can compare them, and how Amperity identifies which tables actually contain personally identifiable information in the first place.

sections.heading: What a Semantic Tag Is
sections.body:
A semantic tag is a label applied to a data field that names what kind of customer-profile information it actually holds — regardless of what the column happens to be called in the source system. A column literally named 'fname' gets tagged given-name; a column called 'lname' gets tagged surname. The documentation is direct about why this matters: 'Semantic tags must be defined for every data source that provides customer profile data to Stitch' — Stitch being Amperity's identity-resolution engine, the process that compares fields across sources to decide which records describe the same person.

The reason tagging has to happen before Stitch runs is that Stitch has no built-in way to know two differently-named columns mean the same thing. One source might store a phone number in a column called 'phone_number,' another in a column called 'cell' or just 'contact.' Left alone, those look like unrelated fields. Tagging both of them 'phone' tells Amperity they're the same kind of data, so Stitch can actually compare them when deciding whether two records match.

sections.heading: Standard Tags and Custom Tags
sections.body:
Amperity ships with a set of standard semantic tags for the fields identity resolution most commonly needs: given-name, surname, phone, and birthdate are the ones called out explicitly, though the standard set extends beyond just these four. Applying a standard tag is the same action regardless of which one it is — you're telling Amperity 'this field, no matter its original column name, means this.'

Beyond the standard set, you can define custom tags — free-text labels like 'loyalty-id' — for anything specific to your own business that doesn't map to a built-in category. A custom tag behaves identically to a standard one once applied: Stitch treats it as a recognized, comparable field across every source where you've used that same tag.

sections.heading: Two Ways to Apply Tags: AmpAI Select vs Manual
sections.body:
There are two paths to getting tags onto your tables. AmpAI Select — the automated option — determines which tables contain the best data for identity resolution and recommends semantic tags for the fields in them, without you having to inspect each column yourself. It also handles one specific cleanup task on its own: converting non-standard date formats it encounters along the way.

The manual path, triggered by choosing 'Manually select,' skips the AI recommendation and puts you directly in control: you apply tags — standard or custom — field by field, typing a tag into the Semantic tags column and pressing ENTER to save it. This is also the only path for tags AmpAI wouldn't know to suggest, since custom tags like 'loyalty-id' are specific to your business and not something a general recommendation engine would guess.

Neither choice is permanent. Tables you've already tagged, whether through AmpAI Select or manually, can be reopened later to review or change the tags applied to them.

sections.heading: Finding Which Tables Actually Contain PII
sections.body:
Tagging assumes you already know which tables are worth tagging in the first place — and that's a separate question Amperity also helps answer. Personally identifiable information, in this context, isn't defined as a fixed checklist of field names; the documentation describes it functionally, as whatever data feeds into building accurate customer identity records. In practice that's the same category of field semantic tags target: names, emails, phone numbers, and similar personal details.

Amperity's Stitch technology uses what the documentation calls 'patented algorithms' to analyze customer data and build what it calls an identity graph — a structure that maps every source record found to belong to the same person onto one shared Amperity ID. The documentation is deliberately non-specific about how the algorithms themselves work; what it does specify is the outcome: an identity graph built from 'accurate and actionable customer profiles.'

Finding PII-bearing tables uses the same two-path choice as tagging. Clicking AmpAI select identifies likely tables, proposes primary keys, and applies semantic tags together, in one pass, rather than as three separate decisions. Clicking 'Manually select' instead puts table selection under your control from the start — and even after using AmpAI select, you can go back and review or override whatever it chose.

sections.heading: How Tagging and PII Discovery Fit Together
sections.body:
Selecting PII-bearing tables and tagging their fields aren't really two separate workflows — they're two views into the same screen. AmpAI select can do both in one motion; manual select walks you through both, one after the other. A table selected but never tagged gives Stitch nothing to standardize against other sources; a field tagged on a table that was never identified as holding real customer data tags something that was never going to matter to identity resolution in the first place.

This also connects directly back to primary keys from the previous course: a table needs both a primary key, so Stitch can track individual rows over time, and semantic tags, so Stitch can compare its fields against equivalent fields elsewhere. A table with one but not the other is only half-ready as input to identity resolution.

quiz.question: Why does Amperity require semantic tags on every source that feeds customer profile data to Stitch?
options: Tags trigger the nightly load schedule; sources without any tags applied never sync automatically.
Tags standardize what a field means, like phone, so Stitch can compare fields across sources.
Tags determine which fields get encrypted at rest; fields left untagged are stored as plain text.
Tags set the display order of columns in the Customer 360 output table used for reporting on customers.

quiz.question: What does AmpAI Select do differently from choosing 'Manually select' on the Identity resolution page?
options: It restricts you to standard tags only, while manual selection is required to add any custom tag.
It applies tags to every table in the account at once, while manual selection is limited to one table.
It requires a separate approval step from an Amperity account manager before any tags take effect.
It automatically finds the best tables for identity resolution and recommends keys and tags for them.

quiz.question: What is the identity graph, as built by Amperity's Stitch process?
options: A structure that maps every source record belonging to the same person onto one shared Amperity ID.
A structure that maps every semantic tag to the source table where it was first defined and used.
A visual dashboard showing which tables in the account still lack a configured primary key entirely.
A structure that maps every excluded value to the row exclusion rule that removed it from view.

title: From Raw Data to a Unified Profile
content: Walks through the four-stage profile generation workflow, how a merge policy resolves conflicting values across sources for a single customer, and the five standard output tables -- Customer 360, Identity Graph, Merged Customers, Unified Coalesced, and Unified Scores -- that generation produces.

sections.heading: What Profile Generation Does and When to Run It
sections.body:
Connecting a source, assigning it a primary key, excluding bad values, and tagging its fields — everything covered in the first three courses — gets data ready to be used. It doesn't, by itself, produce a customer profile. That's a distinct, explicit step: profile generation, run from the Customer profiles page in Quick start by clicking 'Generate profiles' on the Generate tables card.

Profiles need to be regenerated any time a source table containing personally identifiable information changes — a new load, an edited record, a newly tagged field all mean the profiles built from that data are now out of date until generation runs again. That can happen through a scheduled workflow or by triggering it manually from that same button, and it's the step that turns everything upstream — connected sources, keys, exclusions, tags — into an actual unified customer record.

sections.heading: The Four-Stage Generation Workflow
sections.body:
Generation moves through four stages in order. First, domain table updates: the domain tables — Amperity's standardized shape for a category of source data — refresh with whatever has changed in the underlying source tables since the last run. Second, data quality validation: Amperity checks the refreshed source data for specific, concrete problems — invalid phone numbers, missing item quantities, missing revenue figures, whether order and store IDs are actually present in transactions data, and invalid email addresses. This check exists because feeding malformed data into identity matching doesn't just produce a bad field value, it can produce a wrong match or a missed one.

Third, Stitch executes: the identity-resolution process runs against the validated, primary-keyed, semantically tagged data prepared in earlier courses, comparing records across sources to decide which ones describe the same person. Fourth, profile refresh: the resulting unified customer profiles are written into the database, replacing whatever was there from the previous generation run.

Each stage depends on the one before it — validation only means anything because the domain tables were just refreshed, and Stitch only produces trustworthy matches because validation already screened out the records most likely to cause a bad one.

sections.heading: Merge Policy: Choosing the Best Value When Sources Disagree
sections.body:
Once Stitch has linked records from multiple sources to a single Amperity ID, those sources often disagree — one has an old email, another has the current one, a third is missing the field entirely. A merge policy is the rule set that decides which source wins for a given field when that happens. The result lands in the Merged Customers table, which the documentation describes as collecting PII from all source datasets and consolidating it into 'a single customer's best set of profile data' per Amperity ID.

Priority is configured independently for six profile attribute categories: address (address, city, state, postal code, country), birthdate, email, gender, name (full name, given name, surname), and phone. For each category, you rank the tables that supply it, and higher-ranked tables win by default. The behavior when a top-ranked source comes up empty is a cascade: if Table A is ranked above Table B for email and Table A's email field is blank for a given customer, Amperity falls back to Table B's value — and keeps moving down the ranked list of tables for that attribute until it finds a non-null value.

Configuration happens in the Profile Builder: arrange tables in priority order for each of the six attribute groups, define source precedence for any additional semantic tags beyond those six, and save. One prerequisite applies before any of this can take effect: at least one domain table with profile semantic tags already applied has to be available to Stitch, or there's nothing for the merge policy to rank in the first place.

sections.heading: The Five Standard Output Tables
sections.body:
Amperity's guided setup always produces five standard output tables, available to the Segment Editor once generation has run. Customer 360 is the unified view across every point of engagement — given name, surname, email, phone, physical address, city, state, postal code, birthdate, and gender, one row per customer. Identity Graph is the structural table underneath it: it compiles the Unified Coalesced table into a graph mapping each data source to an Amperity ID, with three columns — Amperity ID, Datasource, and Customer Key, where Customer Key is the primary key and all customer keys from that data source coalesced into a single value.

Merged Customers, described in the previous section, groups PII across every source with a broader field set than Customer 360 — Address2, company information, country, full name, generational suffix, loyalty ID, and title in addition to the core fields. Unified Coalesced holds all the PII Stitch has processed, with semantic tags themselves as the column headers rather than source-specific names; the combination of primary key and Datasource uniquely identifies each row in it, the same pairing covered in the primary keys course.

Unified Scores is the odd one out: instead of customer data, it documents how Stitch scored and categorized record comparisons — Amperity ID, Source1, Source2, the primary keys being compared, a score, a match category, and a match type. It's the table to check when you need to understand why Stitch decided two particular records did or didn't belong to the same person, rather than what the resulting profile looks like.

sections.heading: How the Pipeline Connects End to End
sections.body:
Every stage in this course consumes something built in an earlier one. A raw source connected as a courier or Snowflake bridge becomes usable only once it has a primary key and a clean set of exclusions; that same table becomes comparable to other sources only once its fields carry semantic tags. Profile generation's data quality validation stage is checking exactly the kind of fields those tags identified as PII. Stitch's matching runs on the primary keys and tagged fields directly. And the merge policy that decides which source wins a conflict only has something to rank because domain tables with applied tags were already available to it.

The five standard output tables are where all of that becomes visible: primary keys and datasources pair up in Identity Graph and Unified Coalesced exactly as designed in the primary keys course; semantic tags literally become Unified Coalesced's column headers; and Unified Scores exposes the Stitch comparisons that tagging and key selection made possible in the first place. Nothing in profile generation invents new data — it's the step where every earlier setup decision becomes one queryable, unified customer record.

quiz.question: In the merge policy example where Table A is ranked above Table B for the email attribute, what happens if Table A's email field is empty for a given customer?
options: The customer's email field is left blank in Merged Customers, since only the top-ranked table is ever checked.
The customer record is flagged as incomplete and excluded from the next profile generation run entirely.
Amperity falls back to Table B's value, continuing down the ranked list until a non-null value is found.
The merge policy is automatically disabled for that customer's Amperity ID until an admin resolves it.

quiz.question: Which stage of the four-stage profile generation workflow checks source data for problems like invalid email addresses or missing revenue?
options: Profile refresh, which runs last and writes the finished profiles into the customer database.
Data quality validation, which runs after domain tables update and before Stitch executes.
Domain table updates, which only refreshes source data without inspecting its contents at all.
Stitch execution, which matches records but does not evaluate any individual field values.

quiz.question: What distinguishes the Unified Scores table from the other four standard output tables?
options: It stores only excluded values and the row-exclusion rules that removed them from other tables.
It stores the merge policy's source ranking order for each of the six profile attribute categories.
It stores the raw, untagged source files exactly as they were pulled before any courier ran.
It documents how pairs of records were scored and categorized when Stitch compared them.

title: Databases, Domain Tables & Feeds
content: Every table you eventually query in Amperity's Customer 360 database traces back through a specific pipeline: raw source data is configured as a feed, Amperity turns that feed into a domain table, and domain tables are assembled -- through passthrough, SQL, or SQL-template tables -- into the database you actually query. This course walks that pipeline end to end, grounded in Amperity's own documentation on databases, domain tables, feeds, and datasets, so that primary keys, semantic tags, and Spark SQL table-building read as one connected process rather than four separate glossary entries.

sections.heading: A Feed Is a Configuration, Not a File
sections.body:
A feed is not the data itself -- it's the configuration that tells Amperity how to load a specific piece of source data into a domain table, including which columns are required and which columns carry semantic tags for profile (PII) or transaction data. Every feed needs at least one field marked as its primary key: a column, or combination of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in the resulting table. Amperity uses that primary key during UPSERT operations -- the process of inserting a new row or updating an existing one that shares the same key, rather than creating a duplicate.

Because the same primary key can show up more than once across multiple loads of a feed, every feed also needs a field that determines which version of a duplicate record wins. This is the last-updated field, and it can be a datetime column, an integer such as a Unix timestamp, or left for Amperity to generate automatically. When it's automatic, the rule is a simple hierarchy: newly ingested data overwrites what's already there, a later-dated file supersedes an earlier one, and within a single file, the last row for a given key wins.

Finally, a feed needs semantic tags applied to its columns -- labels like profile semantics (names, emails, addresses), key semantics (primary keys, foreign keys, blocking keys), product catalog semantics, and transaction semantics. These tags are what let Amperity treat a column called cust_email in one source and email_addr in another as the same kind of thing. The next course in this track covers semantic tags in depth; for now, the important point is that a feed without correctly applied tags is a feed Stitch -- Amperity's identity resolution workflow, which finds the hidden connections between records across a brand's online and offline customer data and assigns each person a stable Amperity ID -- cannot use reliably.

sections.heading: From Feed to Domain Table
sections.body:
Once a feed is configured and activated, Amperity generates a domain table from it. The Domain Tables section of the Sources page lists every table produced this way, showing its name, record type, and column count. To every domain table, Amperity automatically adds three system-generated columns: _pk, an identifier built from whichever columns were tagged as the primary key; _uuid_pk, a system-generated UUID that helps Amperity distribute work during Stitch processing; and _updated, which carries the last-updated details for that row. These three columns are also available downstream, in passthrough tables inside the customer 360 database.

Domain tables are classified by what kind of records they hold. Customer records are identified by the presence of PII-related semantic tags -- an email list with names and phone numbers is a typical example. Interaction records are identified by transaction, itemized-transaction, product-catalog, or other behavior-related semantic tags, and capture things like purchases, returns, or cart adds. A single domain table may contain both kinds of records; during the Stitch process, customer records and interaction records are split apart into dedicated tables for use inside the customer 360 database.

Sometimes a source table's shape doesn't match what semantic tagging or Stitch expects -- a full name that needs splitting into given and surname, or a date that arrives as three separate year/month/day columns. For that, Amperity supports custom domain tables: a domain table reshaped with Spark SQL (Domain SQL) into a new table that itself acts like a feed, in that you can apply semantic tags, identify a primary key, and make it available to Stitch. The documentation is explicit that a custom domain table should be designed to be as static as possible -- because a change in the source data often means rewriting the SQL that defines it, which can force a complete reload of that data source.

sections.heading: From Domain Table to Database: Three Ways to Build a Table
sections.body:
A domain table isn't yet something you can query for marketing or analytics -- it has to become a table inside a database first, and Amperity supports three ways to do that. The first is a passthrough table, which adds a domain table's data directly into the database with little modification. The table's name defaults to whatever the domain table was called, though it can be renamed. For a passthrough table to be usable in the Segment editor or with campaigns, it must contain an Amperity ID field.

The second method is a SQL table, built with Spark SQL -- described in the docs as "a high performance SQL query engine used by Amperity to ingest data, create domain tables, and extend the outcome of the Stitch process" -- and a SELECT statement that defines the table's schema. This matters most when a table hasn't gone through Stitch and has no Amperity ID of its own: the SQL has to associate the table's existing unique identifier with the Amperity ID some other way. The documentation's own example joins a POS_transactions table to a POS_customers table with a LEFT JOIN, mapping customer_id to amperity_id so the transaction rows can be tied back to a resolved identity.

The third method is a SQL template table, which is really a shortcut on top of the second: Amperity ships complete, ready-to-use SQL that matches the default use case for a given standard table. Templates exist for tables like Customer 360, Customer Attributes, Merged Customers, Unified Coalesced, Unified Customer, Unified Itemized Transactions, Unified Scores, and Unified Transactions, among others, plus a few composite templates such as Customer 360 joined with Transaction Attributes Extended. Templates are the recommended path for standard tables precisely because they encode Amperity's default logic instead of asking each tenant to reinvent it.

sections.heading: Assembling a Database: Templates and Merge Rules
sections.body:
A database is the collection of tables built from some combination of stitched output, passthrough domain tables, and custom domain tables. At least one database in a tenant must be designated the Customer 360 database, but there's no upper limit on how many databases a tenant can have. When creating a new one, three database-level templates are available. The Customer 360 template adds standard tables based on which record types are present: if profile semantic tags are in use, it adds Customer 360, Merged Customers, Unified Coalesced, Unified Customer, and Unified Scores; if transaction semantic tags are in use, it also adds Customer Attributes, Transaction Attributes Extended, Unified Itemized Transactions, and Unified Transactions. The Passthrough template instead creates one table for every domain or custom domain table available for pass-through. The Stitch QA template adds tables specific to quality-checking the Stitch process, such as Detailed Examples and Unified Changes Clusters.

A tenant can run more than one database precisely because different teams need different views of the same underlying identity graph, and that's controlled through merge rules. Each database defines its own rules, written in Spark SQL, for how to merge customer profile data field by field. The docs give three concrete examples of why this flexibility matters: an operations team might prioritize the most common values using deterministic matching; an email marketing team might prioritize values sourced from the email platform using probabilistic matching; a paid media team might want all possible values represented, to maximize match rates when uploading audiences to platforms like Google Ads or Facebook.

Because so much of database assembly runs through hand-written Spark SQL, the SQL editor surfaces validation alerts for patterns that tend to hurt performance -- implicit CROSS JOINs that create unintentional Cartesian products, OVER statements missing a PARTITION BY clause, unescaped backslashes inside regular expressions, and unintentional broadcast joins. Critically, the documentation notes that a validation alert does not mean the SQL is invalid; a query can still be activated despite one, which matters for anyone who has hit a red warning and assumed their table was broken.

sections.heading: Putting the Pipeline Together
sections.body:
Laid end to end, the pipeline runs: a feed is configured with a primary key, a last-updated field, and semantic tags; Amperity turns that feed into a domain table, adding _pk, _uuid_pk, and _updated, and classifying its rows as customer or interaction records (optionally after reshaping through a custom domain table); that domain table becomes a table in a database through a passthrough, SQL, or SQL-template build; and the database itself is assembled from one of three templates, with per-field merge rules controlling how competing values resolve when more than one source contributes to the same customer.

The documentation is explicit about sequencing at the top of this chain, too: it states plainly that the processes for adding customer profiles and adding transactions should be completed before creating the customer 360 database. In practice, that means the feeds carrying profile and transaction data need to be configured, tagged, and ready for Stitch before the database template can produce anything meaningful -- the database step assumes the feed and domain-table work is already done, not the other way around.

Once a database exists, getting data back out runs through Database Exports: each export is given a unique name, a selected list of tables to include, a destination, and an orchestration assignment that controls when it runs. That closes the loop -- a feed's raw rows, several transformation steps later, arrive at a destination as a table a downstream system can actually consume.

quiz.question: A feed's source data contains two rows with the same primary key, loaded on different days with no explicit last-updated column configured. Which row does Amperity keep?
options: Whichever row was loaded first, since Amperity treats the earliest load as authoritative by default
The row from the later-dated file, following Amperity's automatic hierarchy for resolving duplicate keys
Both rows are kept as separate entries, since a domain table cannot deduplicate without an explicit field
Whichever row has more non-null columns filled in, since Amperity scores rows by completeness

quiz.question: Which system-generated column does Amperity add to every domain table specifically to help distribute work during Stitch processing?
options: _pk, an identifier generated from the columns associated with the primary key
_updated, a field that only records the datetime a row was first ingested
_uuid_pk, a system-generated UUID used to distribute work during Stitch
_stitch_id, a cluster identifier assigned once identity resolution completes

quiz.question: Per the documentation, what is required for a passthrough table to be usable in the Segment editor and with campaigns?
options: It must contain an Amperity ID field, since that's what campaigns and the Segment editor key on
It must be rebuilt as a SQL table, since passthrough tables cannot be used with campaigns at all
It must exclude every column that carries a PII-related semantic tag before activation
It must be assigned to the Stitch QA template rather than the Customer 360 template

title: A Tour of the Standard Output Tables
content: Amperity's Customer 360 database ships with roughly thirty standard output tables, each documented on its own reference page. This course does not attempt to cover all thirty -- instead it takes five of the most conceptually load-bearing tables and organizes them by what they're for: establishing a single customer identity, exposing the mechanics behind that identity resolution, standardizing PII for audience-building, and describing customer behavior through transactions and loyalty. The remaining tables stay available as reference material once the shape of these five makes sense; think of this as the tour that tells you which reference page to reach for later, not a replacement for any of them.

sections.heading: Why ~30 Tables, and How to Read Them
sections.body:
A Customer 360 database's tables fall into three broad groups. Standard tables form the foundation and include names like Customer 360, Merged Customers, Unified Coalesced, Unified Customer, Unified Transactions, Unified Itemized Transactions, and Unified Scores -- these are the tables Amperity ships templates for, and they're the same across most tenants. Source and custom tables make raw source data and custom domain tables available inside the database as passthrough tables; these vary tenant to tenant, since they reflect whatever behavioral, clickstream, or campaign-response data a given brand actually has. QA tables support the Stitch quality-assurance process and mostly matter to the people tuning identity resolution itself, not to everyday querying.

This course covers five standard tables, chosen because each answers a different question a marketer or analyst actually asks. Customer 360 answers "who is this person, in one row." Unified Coalesced answers "how did Stitch arrive at that row, and what did it merge together." The PII table answers "how do I get clean, standardized contact fields for an audience upload." Unified Transactions and Unified Loyalty answer "what has this person done, at the level of a single order and at the level of a loyalty relationship." Every one of these tables is built using the passthrough, SQL, or SQL-template mechanisms introduced earlier in this track -- Customer 360 itself, for instance, is typically built as a passthrough from the Merged Customers table.

sections.heading: Customer 360 -- the Unified View
sections.body:
The Customer 360 table is the unified view of a customer across every point of engagement, including attributes that cross systems. Each row represents one complete individual: their Amperity ID, their merged PII, and a set of summary attributes. It does not exist by default -- it has to be created, and the recommended way is applying the Customer 360 template when setting up the database, which builds it as a passthrough from the Merged Customers table.

Its standard columns include Amperity ID (String), Given Name and Surname (String), Email and Phone (String), Address, City, State, and Postal (String), Birthdate (Date), and Gender (String) -- the same profile fields that also show up in Merged Customers, Unified Coalesced, Unified Customer, and Unified Preprocessed Raw. Beyond the base profile fields, typical attributes fall into four groups: profile information (names, addresses, email, phone); interactions by channel (e-commerce, point of sale, loyalty); insights (lifetime value, transaction frequency, recency); and predictions (next best purchase, next best action, churn likelihood).

The table also supports optional SHA-256 hashed PII columns -- hashed email and hashed phone -- where SHA-256 is a one-way hashing algorithm that turns a value like an email address into a fixed-length string that can be matched against a platform's own hash of the same value without either side ever transmitting the raw address. That's what lets a hashed-email or hashed-phone column from Customer 360 be uploaded directly as a CSV audience file to platforms like Pinterest Ads or Reddit Ads, without exposing the underlying PII in the file itself.

sections.heading: Unified Coalesced -- Where Identity Resolution Shows Its Work
sections.body:
To understand Unified Coalesced you need Stitch: Amperity's identity resolution workflow, which compares records across every data source a brand provides and decides which ones belong to the same real person, assigning that person a stable Amperity ID. Unified Coalesced is where you can see that process's inputs and intermediate decisions. It consolidates all PII data that passed through Stitch, using semantic tags as its column headers -- and its defining property is that a unique Amperity ID may appear in more than one row. Unlike Customer 360, it doesn't aggregate a person down to a single row; it preserves individual source records, because the whole point of the table is letting you trace how those records were grouped.

The combination of PK and Datasource columns uniquely identifies a row in Unified Coalesced, and that combination correlates back to a single row in a domain table -- so a specific record here can always be traced to the exact source row it came from. Alongside standard PII columns (Name, Address, Email, Phone, Gender, Birthdate), the table carries columns that exist specifically to expose identity-resolution mechanics: Rep DS and Rep PK identify "qualified trivial duplications" -- records with an identity score of 3.0 or greater, representing early, high-confidence groupings Stitch made before the full comparison process ran. Component ID references groupings formed during hierarchical comparison. Is Supersized and Supersized ID flag clusters that grew unusually large, which is often a sign of a data-quality problem rather than a real household or individual. Has BLV and its per-field companions flag values that were removed by the blocklist. CK, a customer-key column, appears only in this table and in Unified Customer.

In practice, Unified Coalesced gets used for three things: verifying that semantic tags were applied correctly and are visible on the Queries page, investigating why particular records ended up in the same (or different) clusters during identity resolution, and examining which values got blocklisted and why. It shows up in Customer 360 databases, in dedicated Stitch QA databases, and in custom databases where someone specifically needs this level of detail.

sections.heading: The PII Table -- Standardizing Identity for Audiences
sections.body:
PII -- personally identifiable information, meaning any data field that could identify a specific individual, like a name, email, or phone number -- is scattered across Unified Coalesced in whatever form each source happened to provide it. The PII table exists to fix that: it collects customer profile data from Unified Coalesced and standardizes it into consistent, predictable values, specifically so that it can be queried to build audiences through the Segment Editor.

The standardization is concrete, not cosmetic. Phone numbers have empty values removed and are reformatted consistently, with a "+1" prefix added and non-numeric characters stripped. State values are only accepted if they're exactly two characters; anything longer or abbreviated differently is excluded rather than guessed at. Gender is standardized down to a lowercase "m" or "f," with any other value converted to null rather than left ambiguous. The resulting columns include amperity_id, given_name, surname, full_name, generational_suffix, email, phone, address, address_line_2, city, state, postal, birthdate, gender, and company.

The clearest use case in the documentation is matching: querying the widest possible range of email addresses associated with a person to help identify which specific address they actually use to log into Facebook or Google, since ad platforms match on exact values. From there, the PII table feeds data templates that reshape its output for a specific destination -- Facebook, Google, and Braze are named explicitly -- so the same standardized table can support consistent audience queries across multiple external platforms instead of each destination needing its own bespoke extract.

sections.heading: Unified Transactions and Unified Loyalty -- Behavior at Two Grains
sections.body:
Unified Transactions holds one row per unique transaction record, with every order ID associated to an Amperity ID. It's mandatory whenever a tenant has transaction and itemized-transaction data available, and it has to be built in a specific order: Unified Itemized Transactions first, then Unified Transactions, then Transaction Attributes Extended -- because Unified Transactions is built by rolling up and aggregating the item-level rows in Unified Itemized Transactions into one row per order. Its roughly thirty columns include Order ID (the primary key), Order Datetime, Order Revenue, Order Quantity, Purchase Channel, Store ID, and Customer ID, which joins to Amperity ID when no foreign key already links the two. A dedicated SQL section called amp_priority handles the edge case where a single order ID ends up associated with more than one Amperity ID, resolving it by update date and Amperity ID order.

Four optional attribute sets can be switched on in the SQL template: fiscal calendars, which align order dates to a brand's accounting periods instead of the calendar year; net order revenue, calculated as revenue across all items including returns and cancellations but excluding discounts; order costs, representing total cost of goods sold minus returns, cancellations, and discounts, which requires cost data tagged in Unified Itemized Transactions; and order discount amounts, totaled either with a MAX() or a SUM() depending on whether the source data records one discount per order or prorates it across items.

Unified Loyalty operates at a different grain: one row per combination of Amperity ID and Loyalty ID, since a single customer can belong to multiple loyalty programs, or hold multiple accounts within one program. It's optional and is typically built as a passthrough table. For a loyalty profile to reach full Amperity ID uniqueness, three semantic-tagging conditions have to hold: the fk-loyalty-id tag matches the loyalty ID field, the loy/email tag is applied to the email field, and the loy/birthdate tag is applied to the birthdate field. Its nineteen columns cover required fields (Loyalty ID, Is Opted-in, Latest Opted-in Datetime), tier information (Current Tier, Spend To Next Tier, Spend To Keep Tier), balance data (Current Balance, Lifetime Balance), and enrollment and activity tracking. The documentation's own examples use it for retention analysis -- comparing churn between loyalty members and non-members by enrollment period -- and value analysis, comparing twelve-month revenue and order frequency across the same groups.

quiz.question: According to the documentation, what makes Unified Coalesced different from Customer 360?
options: Unified Coalesced aggregates every source record for a customer into a single merged row
Unified Coalesced excludes all PII and stores only numeric Stitch confidence scores
Unified Coalesced only contains records that Stitch failed to match to any identity
Unified Coalesced preserves individual source rows, so one Amperity ID can appear twice

quiz.question: Per the documentation, what does the PII table do with a phone number field pulled from Unified Coalesced?
options: It discards phone numbers entirely, since phone is not considered PII in this table
It removes empty values and reformats the number consistently, adding a "+1" prefix
It leaves phone numbers untouched, deferring all formatting to the destination platform
It converts phone numbers into a SHA-256 hash before they reach the PII table

quiz.question: Why must Unified Itemized Transactions be built before Unified Transactions, per the documentation?
options: Unified Loyalty tier calculations depend on itemized transaction data being present first
The PII table cannot standardize phone numbers until itemized transactions are loaded
Amperity IDs are only assigned to customers after itemized transactions finish processing
Unified Transactions rolls up and aggregates the itemized rows into one row per order

title: Semantic Tags & Data Types
content: Two mechanisms sit underneath everything else in this track: semantic tags, which give Amperity a common vocabulary for the same kind of field even when every source names and shapes it differently, and data types, which define what a field is allowed to hold before that vocabulary can be applied to it. This course, grounded in Amperity's semantic-tag and data-type reference documentation, covers both -- what tags exist, how they're assigned, what types Amperity supports, and the specific rule for handling data that doesn't come in a flat, simple shape.

sections.heading: What a Semantic Tag Does
sections.body:
A semantic tag is a label that standardizes personally identifiable information (PII), transaction data, and other important customer-profile details across every column in every source table a tenant has. The problem it solves is that two data sources describing the same kind of information -- a customer's email address, say -- will almost never use the same column name, the same casing, or the same data quality. A semantic tag gives Amperity a common understanding of what a field means, independent of what it happens to be called.

That matters because of how it changes the work required to bring new data in. Traditional integration often relies on ETL -- extract, transform, load -- where data is cleaned and reshaped to match a target schema before it's ever loaded into the destination system. Semantic tags let Amperity work the other way around, as ELT: extract, load, transform. Raw data can be handed to Amperity largely as-is, loaded into a domain table, and then tagged -- with the transformation (standardizing formats, splitting names, resolving identity) happening inside Amperity after loading, rather than as an expensive preprocessing step a source system has to perform first.

Because Stitch, Amperity's identity resolution process, relies on accurate semantic tagging to run its blocking strategies -- the comparison shortcuts it uses to avoid checking every record against every other record -- a mistagged or untagged field doesn't just look wrong in a report. It can directly degrade how well Stitch resolves identity across sources.

sections.heading: The Tag Categories
sections.body:
Profile and PII tags cover the fields that describe a person: email (with variants like email-primary and email-alternate), phone (phone-home, phone-mobile, phone-work), given-name, surname, full-name, address and its components (address2, city, state, postal), and birthdate. These are the tags that feed the Customer 360 and PII tables covered earlier in this track.

Key tags describe how records relate to each other and to an identity. A primary key (pk) uniquely identifies a row within its own table. A foreign key (fk-[namespace]) points from one table to a customer identity defined elsewhere. A customer key (ck) marks a field specifically used to represent customer identity. A separation key (sk-[semantic]) is used to keep certain records from being merged together during Stitch even if other fields would otherwise suggest they match -- useful for cases like shared family email addresses. A blocking key (bk-[label]) feeds Stitch's blocking strategies directly, grouping records into smaller comparison sets so identity resolution doesn't have to compare every record in a table against every other record.

Interaction tags cover transaction and itemized-transaction data, plus loyalty-specific tags prefixed loy/ for profile-level loyalty fields and loy-event/ for loyalty activity events. Product catalog tags are prefixed pc/ and cover fields like product ID and category. System tags exist too -- update-dt is the one named in the documentation, used to track when a record was most recently updated.

sections.heading: Assigning Tags and Handling Multiple Values
sections.body:
Tags are applied through the Feed Editor: open a data source's feed, select Edit, and Amperity will have already applied some tags automatically based on column names and content. From there, the person configuring the feed reviews those automatic tags for accuracy and manually applies tags to whatever fields are left, before clicking Activate to make the feed live.

Some tags carry a data-type requirement, which is where this course's second half connects to its first: fields tagged postal or phone must be a String type, and fields tagged birthdate must be a Date type. If a field's actual type doesn't match what its tag requires, Amperity blocks the save with an error rather than silently coercing the value -- which is a deliberate guardrail, since a birthdate stored as a string could sort or compare incorrectly downstream.

When a single source has more than one instance of the same kind of field -- two email columns, three phone columns -- the same tag gets applied to each field, and then a suffix distinguishes them. The recommended approach is a namespace, like email-primary and email-alternate, which produces readable column names such as email_primary and email_alternate once the data reaches the Unified Coalesced table. The alternative is an ordinal, like email-1 and email-2, producing columns named email_1 and phone_2. Namespaces are preferred specifically because the resulting column names describe what the field actually is, not just its position in a list.

sections.heading: Data Types: The Simple Types
sections.body:
Amperity defines seven simple data types, each with a direct equivalent in the major platforms it integrates with. Boolean holds TRUE, FALSE, or NULL. Date holds an ISO-8601 compliant date value, like 2021-11-04. Datetime holds an ISO-8601 compliant date and time value, used for things like transaction timestamps. Decimal holds a fixed-point number with a configurable number of digits before and after the decimal point -- the right choice for prices, where floating-point rounding error is unacceptable. Float holds a floating-point number, appropriate where exact precision matters less than range. Integer holds a whole number of various lengths, explicitly not intended for prices. String holds a sequence of characters -- names, emails, addresses, UUIDs, phone numbers, and free-text descriptions all fall here.

These line up with familiar equivalents elsewhere: Decimal corresponds to DECIMAL(p,s) in Databricks and BigQuery or NUMBER(p,s) in Snowflake; Integer spans BIGINT, INT, SMALLINT, and TINYINT across those platforms; String matches STRING, VARCHAR, and CHAR. That mapping exists because Amperity ingests data that originated in one of those systems, and getting the type right at the boundary is what makes the postal/phone/birthdate tagging rules from the previous section enforceable in the first place -- a type mismatch there isn't a formatting nuisance, it's a save-blocking error.

sections.heading: Complex Types and the Conversion Rule
sections.body:
Beyond the simple types, Amperity recognizes three composite data types that source systems sometimes use to nest data inside a single field. An Array stores a sequence of elements, where each element is itself a set of fields and values. A Map stores data as key-value pairs. A Struct groups data as a sequence of fields within one structure -- effectively an object nested inside a column.

Amperity will load a source containing any of these types into a domain table without complaint, but that's as far as they can go unmodified: none of the three can be used directly with Stitch or have semantic tags applied to them as-is. Instead, the fix is the same custom domain table mechanism introduced earlier in this track. A custom domain table, written in Spark SQL, converts every element of the array, map, or struct into its own individual field in the table's output -- at which point semantic tags and keys can be assigned to those individual fields exactly like any other column. Composite types are allowed to appear in a common table expression partway through that SQL, as long as the final query output contains no array, map, or struct fields by the time it's produced.

A small number of source-platform types don't have a path into Amperity at all as semi-structured data: Google BigQuery's RANGE type, and Snowflake's FILE, VARIANT, and VECTOR types among others. These have to be converted to one of the fully structured types -- simple or composite -- before Amperity will accept them, for the same underlying reason arrays and structs need conversion: everything downstream, from semantic tagging to Stitch to the standard output tables covered elsewhere in this track, assumes a flat, typed column to work with.

quiz.question: Why does Amperity's use of semantic tags support ELT (extract, load, transform) instead of traditional ETL?
options: Tags let raw data load as-is, with reshaping happening afterward instead of before loading
Tags automatically convert every source column to Amperity's preferred naming scheme on load
Tags are optional under ETL, but they only become mandatory once a tenant adopts an ELT pipeline
Tags replace the need for a primary key by inferring row uniqueness from field content alone

quiz.question: A source table has two phone number columns. What does the documentation recommend for tagging them?
options: Apply the phone tag to one column only, and drop the second column entirely during ingestion
Merge both phone columns into a single combined string field before any tag is applied
Apply the phone tag to both fields, then append a namespace like phone-home and phone-mobile
Leave both phone fields untagged, since Stitch can only compare one phone field per source

quiz.question: Per the documentation, what has to happen before a struct-typed field can be assigned a semantic tag?
options: Nothing -- semantic tags can be applied directly to struct fields without any conversion step
It must be dropped from the domain table, since Stitch cannot process any composite type
It must be loaded into Unified Coalesced first, where each struct element becomes its own row
It must be converted to individual fields in a custom domain table, which can then be tagged

title: Building Segments
content: A segment is the audience-defining building block underneath every campaign and journey in Amperity: an attribute profile built in the Segment Editor whose matching customers become your marketing audience. This course walks through how segments are assembled from tenant data, how AND/OR logic and activation IDs shape which customers qualify, how to read the insights that tell you whether a segment is any good before you send anything, and how AmpAI's Customer Data Assistant can generate a starting segment from a plain-language goal instead of a blank editor.

sections.heading: What a Segment Is, and Where You Build It
sections.body:
A segment defines a specific attribute profile, and the customers who match that profile make up the segment's audience. Everything downstream -- campaigns, journeys, exports -- starts from one or more segments, which is why the Segment Editor is the first tool worth understanding in this track. You reach it two ways: the "Create Segment" button on the Segments page opens the full editor with segment insights attached, or the "Add sub-audience" link inside a campaign opens a related but reduced tool called Audience Builder, which shares the same condition-building interface but does not show insights and is limited to the database and tables already used to build the campaign's starting audience.

Segments are built against tables in your customer 360 database -- the unified store Amperity maintains after resolving and merging customer records from your source systems. Amperity provides several standard tables that are always available to the Segment Editor: Customer 360 (profile data like names, addresses, emails, and phone numbers, summarized one row per unique customer), Unified Transactions (order-level purchase details), Unified Itemized Transactions (line-item and product catalog details within those orders), and Transaction Attributes Extended (calculated fields built on top of the order- and item-level data, such as recency and monetary scores). Depending on your tenant, Campaign Recipients, Customer Attributes, and -- where predictive modeling is enabled -- Predicted Affinity and Predicted CLV Attributes tables are also available. You can expand any table row in the editor to see its attributes, or open the Data Explorer for detailed attribute descriptions and example values.

One tenant-level setting changes what a segment actually counts: the activation ID. This is the field a segment resolves its audience against -- commonly a customer-level Amperity ID, but a tenant can configure others, such as an email_id. Switching the Segment Editor's Activation ID dropdown to email_id restricts the available tables and lists to only those containing a matching email_id field, and it changes the editor's own language to match: "Include customers with ALL of the following" becomes "Include email addresses with ALL of the following" once the plural name for that activation ID is "email addresses." The same customer can appear multiple times in an email_id-activated segment if they have more than one address on file, which is a different shape of audience than a one-row-per-customer segment.

sections.heading: Choosing Attributes and Reading Segment Insights
sections.body:
Once you've picked a table, you build a segment by adding attributes -- individual fields, like Predicted Lifecycle Status or Total Value of Orders -- and configuring how each one should filter the audience. Attributes come from four sources: tables in the customer 360 database (standard or custom), purchase behaviors, custom tables built in the Queries page and made available to the Segment Editor, and files uploaded directly to the editor. Purchase behaviors are a distinct category worth calling out on their own: attributes like First Purchase, Has Purchased, Has Not Purchased, Most Frequent Order, Repeat Purchase, and Total Value of Orders combine a customer's interaction history with your product catalog, and they only work if your tenant uses Amperity's standard field names for that catalog data.

Some attributes take a value immediately -- boolean (true/false) attributes are the common case -- while most string, date, time, amount, and quantity attributes expose additional configuration fields once you've added them, such as an operator and a comparison value. A churn-prevention segment might start with Predicted Lifecycle Status, which has six possible stages, and use the "is in list" operator to select "Active," "Cooling down," and "At risk" in one condition, then add a second attribute -- Has Purchased, scoped to the previous three months -- to narrow further.

After adding an attribute, clicking Refresh recalculates segment insights, which answer four standing questions about whatever audience you've defined so far: Unique Customers (the count by unique Amperity ID), 1-year Active Customers (unique customers who purchased within the past year), 1-year Segment Revenue (total revenue from those active customers over the same window), and Reachable Customers (unique customers with at least one contactable email address, phone number, or physical mailing address). Before you've added any conditions, these numbers represent 100% of your customer base; each attribute you add and refresh narrows them, which is what lets you watch an audience shrink or grow in real time as you build. Reachable does not mean opted in -- a customer can have a contactable email on file without having consented to receive marketing at it, a distinction that matters once you get to campaigns.

sections.heading: Combining Conditions: Inclusions, Exclusions, and AND/OR Logic
sections.body:
Every segment starts from the full customer 360 database and narrows down through inclusions and exclusions. An inclusion is a condition that determines which customers belong in the audience; an exclusion is a condition that determines which customers get removed from it, even if they'd otherwise match. Both inclusions and exclusions can reference customer lists as well as attributes -- a customer list can be a saved query, another existing segment, or a file of customer identifiers uploaded to Amperity, which is how you layer "everyone who matches these attributes, except anyone already on this suppression list" into a single segment.

How multiple conditions combine is controlled by AND and OR, which behave exactly as they do in SQL: AND requires a customer to match every condition it joins, which always produces an audience the same size or smaller than any single condition alone; OR requires a customer to match only one of the conditions it joins, which always produces an audience the same size or larger. A segment built on City = "Chicago" alone returns Chicago residents. Add State = "Illinois" with AND and you get the same result, since Chicago residents are already Illinois residents -- but change that AND to OR and the audience grows to every Chicago resident plus every Illinois resident statewide, including people in Springfield or Peoria who've never set foot in Chicago. The default connector in the Segment Editor is AND; a slider switches a given connection to OR, and this choice can be set independently within a group of attributes and between separate groups of attributes.

That distinction matters most when an attribute value isn't unique on its own. "Madison" is a city name that exists in more than twenty U.S. states, so a segment filtering City = "Madison" without qualification will pull in residents of Madison, Wisconsin and Madison, Indiana and every other Madison indiscriminately. Pairing it with the right state using AND -- City = "Madison" AND State = "Wisconsin" -- resolves the ambiguity; pairing two such qualified groups with OR, like (Madison AND Wisconsin) OR (Madison AND Indiana), lets you target both specific cities at once without picking up every other Madison in the country.

sections.heading: Letting AmpAI Draft a Starting Segment
sections.body:
Amperity's documentation describes a conversational entry point called the Customer Data Assistant, part of AmpAI, that works from a plain-language description of intent rather than from picklists: "describe what you want to accomplish and it generates segments or journeys from scratch." Instead of opening the Segment Editor and choosing a starting table and attribute yourself, you describe the audience you want -- the documentation's own framing is working "from intent" to a concrete output -- and the assistant produces a segment definition as a starting point.

The documented workflow treats this as a draft, not a finished artifact: "a typical workflow might start with using the Customer Data Assistant to create a segment and journey, and then using the Manual edit option to open the specialized editors." In other words, the assistant's output lands you back in the same Segment Editor covered earlier in this course, with a set of attributes and conditions already populated from your description, ready for you to inspect, adjust, and -- critically -- refresh for segment insights before you'd trust it as an audience for a campaign. The assistant shortens the path to a first draft; it doesn't remove the verification step.

One documented limitation is worth knowing before you rely on this heavily: a custom prompt "provides context but the Segment assistant and Journey assistant have their own specialized logic" that isn't fully overridden by whatever extra instructions you supply. Practically, that means the assistant is best treated as a fast way to get a reasonable starting set of conditions for a stated goal -- not as a tool you can steer arbitrarily through prompt engineering to produce an exact, unusual condition structure. For that, the Segment Editor's own manual controls -- attributes, operators, AND/OR logic -- remain the precise instrument.

sections.heading: Naming and Saving Your Segment
sections.body:
Once a segment's insights look right, Save As opens a naming dialog, and the name you choose matters more than it might seem, because segments get reused and referenced across a tenant by people who weren't the ones who built them -- and, downstream, by teams working in destination platforms like Braze, Klaviyo, or Facebook Ads who never see the Segment Editor at all. An auto-generated name like "Untitled segment (43) - 2021-08-13-09-34-35" tells none of those people anything about who's in it or why it exists.

The documented conventions: describe the audience and purpose directly ("Dormant Customers," "High_CLV_Historical"), append qualifiers like "historical," "daily," or "test" when a segment is one of several similar variants, and include brand or region names once a tenant manages more than one of either -- "Birthdays_Under_40_CA" and "Birthdays_Under_40_NY" as separate, unambiguous segments rather than one generically named segment reused for two purposes. If a segment lives in a folder, prefixing its name with the folder name keeps it identifiable even outside that folder's context -- "Braze_Birthdays_Under_40_CA" for a segment filed under a "Braze" folder. For sequential naming, leading zeros ("0001," "0002") keep segments sorted in the intended order both inside Amperity and in whatever downstream platform lists them alphabetically.

After saving, the Segment Overview page opens automatically and adds detail beyond the four core insights: historical and predicted revenue, the percentage of customers reachable by email, phone, or Facebook, and customer trends such as purchases by channel and revenue by lifetime spend.
