It's worth remembering the same caveat from segment insights applies here too -- reachable customers may not have opted into marketing through that channel, so a high reachability percentage describes contact data on file, not consent to use it.

quiz.question: In the Segment Editor, what changes when a tenant's activation ID is switched from a default customer-level ID to "email_id"?
options: Only tables with a matching email_id field remain available, and the editor's language switches from customers to email addresses.
Only tables with a matching phone number field remain available, and the editor's language switches from customers to phone numbers.
Segment insights and refresh counts stop displaying until an entirely different customer 360 database is selected for the tenant.
Every attribute already added to the segment is removed automatically and must be reselected manually under the new activation mapping.

quiz.question: A segment combines two attribute groups: (city OR state) joined by AND to (opted into email OR opted into SMS). Based on how AND/OR logic works in the Segment Editor, what happens to audience size?
options: Both groups shrink individually because OR narrows results within each group, and AND then narrows the audience further between the two groups.
Each group grows larger on its own because OR broadens matches, but AND between the two groups narrows the result to customers matching both.
Each group grows larger on its own because OR broadens matches, and AND between the two groups also broadens the combined audience even further.
Both groups shrink individually because AND applies first within each group, and OR between the two groups then broadens the combined result.

quiz.question: According to Amperity's documentation, what is the typical relationship between the Customer Data Assistant and the Segment Editor when building a segment from a plain-language goal?
options: The Customer Data Assistant replaces the Segment Editor entirely once activation IDs are configured correctly for a tenant.
The Customer Data Assistant only becomes available after a segment has already been built manually inside the Segment Editor.
A typical workflow starts with the Customer Data Assistant generating a segment from a description, then Manual edit refines it.
The Customer Data Assistant requires a custom prompt that fully overrides the Segment assistant's own built-in specialized logic.

title: Running Campaigns
content: A campaign is how a segment's audience actually leaves Amperity and reaches customers: it takes the audience a segment defines, splits it into sub-audiences aligned to marketing strategy, routes each sub-audience to one or more destinations, and schedules when that happens. This course covers building a campaign from a segment, structuring sub-audiences with treatment and control groups, how destination timing and requirements vary by platform, and orchestrations -- the parallel, query-based path for sending data out of Amperity when a campaign's segment-driven structure isn't the right shape for the job.

sections.heading: From Segment to Campaign Audience
sections.body:
A campaign is defined in the documentation as a message or offer sent to a specific group of customers or recipients. Where a segment answers "who matches this profile," a campaign answers "what do we send this audience, and where." Every campaign starts the same way: choose one or more segments from the Include dropdown, and those customers become the campaign's audience. If you started with a single segment, that choice pays off later -- you can reuse that segment's own insights to track the campaign audience's performance over time, rather than recalculating everything from scratch inside the campaign.

Exclude works the same way in reverse: choosing one or more segments from the Exclude dropdown removes any customer who matches them, which is how SMS opt-outs or email unsubscribe lists get kept out of a send without rebuilding the include logic to account for them. When multiple exclusion segments are used together, they combine with OR -- a customer is excluded if they match any one of the exclusion segments, not only if they match all of them.

The activation ID a campaign uses is inherited from whichever segment defines its starting audience, and any additional segments used for inclusion or exclusion must share that same activation ID -- you can't mix an email-activated segment into a campaign whose starting audience is customer-ID activated. As with the Segment Editor, the campaign's own language updates to match -- "Customers" becomes "Email addresses" where appropriate. Campaign naming carries real downstream weight: the campaign name always appears in the filename sent to every destination, so names like "Acme_Churn" or "Birthdays_Under_40" that stay consistent across treatment groups and sub-audiences make files identifiable in a destination platform where nobody sees the campaign builder itself.

sections.heading: Sub-Audiences, Treatment Groups, and Control Groups
sections.body:
Not every campaign needs to send one message to one undivided audience. A sub-audience is a list of customers who receive a specific communication within a larger campaign -- split out by brand, product affinity, lifecycle stage, or any other attribute the strategy calls for. You create one by clicking Add Sub-Audience, which opens Audience Builder -- the same condition-building interface as the Segment Editor, minus segment insights, scoped to the database and tables already in use. A documented example builds three sub-audiences off Predicted Lifecycle Status from the Predicted CLV Attributes table: one for "Active," named "Active_Socks"; one for "Cooling down," named "CoolingDown_Socks"; one for "At risk," named "AtRisk_Socks." A campaign supports up to 60 sub-audiences.

Every treatment group's name concatenates with the campaign name to form the filename that ultimately reaches a destination: {{ campaign_name }}_{{ recipient_group_name }}. A campaign named "Churn_HighValue_Early" with a "CoolingDown_Socks" treatment group produces the filename "Churn_HighValue_Early_CoolingDown_Socks" -- which is why treatment group names are meant to build on the campaign name rather than duplicate or contradict it.

A treatment group is the percentage of an audience that receives the campaign's communications; a control group is the percentage that deliberately does not, held back as a randomized sample from the original audience so you have a baseline to measure the campaign's actual effect over time. A campaign typically has one control group overall unless sub-audiences are defined, in which case each sub-audience can carry its own. Amperity attempts, but does not guarantee, consistent control group membership across sends of a recurring campaign -- when the audience size holds steady, the same customers tend to stay in the control group; when it changes, IDs are added or removed to match, and individual customers can shift between control and treatment across sends. On a small audience, setting the control group percentage below roughly 10% risks landing at zero control customers by chance, which defeats the point of having a baseline -- the documented fix is simply moving the percentage closer to 10%.

sections.heading: Destinations, Timing, and Campaign Types
sections.body:
A destination is where a sub-audience's list actually lands, and destinations vary in what data they require. Klaviyo requires an email address, plus whatever additional profile data (birthdays, preferences) you choose to attach; Criteo requires only email; TikTok Ads requires both email and phone number, and optionally accepts Apple and Android advertising IDs; Attentive Mobile requires either a phone number or an email address depending on how that instance is configured; Facebook Ads requires strict field mapping and naming conventions. The documentation recommends sourcing customer PII for these sends from the Merged Customers table specifically, describing it as Amperity's most accurate and complete source of customer PII.

How fast an audience actually shows up at its destination depends on the destination type, not on the campaign. Cloud storage and file-transfer destinations -- Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, SFTP -- typically resolve within about an hour. Email service providers and marketing automation platforms -- ActiveCampaign, Braze, HubSpot, Klaviyo, Salesforce Marketing Cloud -- typically take 12 to 24 hours. Paid media platforms -- Amazon Ads, Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, The Trade Desk, Reddit Ads, Snapchat, TikTok Ads Manager -- typically take the longest, 24 to 48 hours. A launch date planned around a paid-media deadline needs to account for that lag; the same campaign reaching an S3 bucket has much more slack.

Campaigns come in three documented shapes. One-time campaigns send a specific message exactly once, such as a welcome message for a new loyalty member. Recurring campaigns automatically refresh and resend an audience on a defined cadence -- daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly -- keyed off a state change like a loyalty tier update or a return. Multichannel campaigns blend the same strategy across several channels at once, using sub-audiences to partition the single starting audience by channel, with each sub-audience potentially carrying its own control group. Before any of these actually schedules, the Campaign Test dialog lets you set a sample record count and run a test send that outputs a sample file showing what downstream systems would actually receive.

sections.heading: Orchestrations: The Query-Based Path to a Destination
sections.body:
Not everything that needs to leave Amperity is a segment-driven marketing audience -- sometimes what a destination needs is the result of an arbitrary query, or an entire database export, and that's what an orchestration is for. An orchestration is the configured relationship between a data source -- either an active query written in Presto SQL, or a database export configured on the Customer 360 page -- and a destination, plus how often that relationship runs. Where a campaign always starts from one or more segments, an orchestration starts from a query or an export; the two are separate mechanisms for the same underlying goal of getting data out of Amperity and into a destination.

Setting one up starts on the Destinations page, using the "Add Orchestration" button, which opens the New Orchestration dialog. From there: pick an Object Type of either Query or Database Export; pick the specific Object -- the query or export by name, which also becomes the orchestration's own name; pick the Destination the data should land in; and pick a Data Template, which defines how the results get formatted for that destination. A documented example sends query results to Domo using a "Domo S3" destination and a "Domo S3 CSV Files for Dashboards" template, landing the data in a customer-managed Amazon S3 bucket that Domo then loads as a dataset -- with the template already preconfigured correctly, requiring no further setup in that case.

Every orchestration also has a run mode -- Manual or Automatic -- and the documentation's recommendation is consistent with the Campaign Test workflow covered above: start with Manual so you can confirm the orchestration actually produces correct output at the destination, then switch it to Automatic once you trust it. An orchestration cannot be created against a query that's still in draft status; the query has to be active first. Because a destination and a data template can each be reused by more than one orchestration, a tenant with several recurring exports typically ends up with a handful of destinations and templates feeding many orchestrations, rather than a unique destination configuration per export.

sections.heading: Testing and Monitoring Before You Schedule
sections.body:
Both paths covered in this course -- campaigns and orchestrations -- share the same underlying discipline: verify before you automate. A campaign's Campaign Test dialog and an orchestration's Manual-first setting exist for the same reason, catching mapping errors, missing fields, or wrong destination configuration before a real audience or a recurring schedule depends on it.

Amperity also monitors already-scheduled work and surfaces problems automatically. Email notifications alert users to campaign delivery issues -- the documentation cites two concrete examples: a Facebook Ads send missing required external identifiers, and a Google Ads destination with two-factor authentication disabled, both of which would silently block delivery if left unaddressed. These notifications describe the problem, outline resolution steps, and link back to the Workflows page, where the underlying send or orchestration run can actually be inspected and corrected.

Once a campaign is scheduled, clicking the Schedule button in the top right of the Campaigns page is the final step -- everything before it (audience, exclusions, sub-audiences, destinations, timing, launch date, and a passed test) is what makes that click safe to make. The same logic applies to flipping an orchestration from Manual to Automatic: it's the last step, not the first one, in a workflow that starts with proving the output is correct.

quiz.question: A campaign is configured with a 5% control group on a very small sub-audience. Per Amperity's documentation on control groups, what should a marketer expect and do about it?
options: The control group will always contain at least one customer no matter how small the audience is, so no adjustment is needed.
Amperity automatically raises the control percentage to 10 percent whenever an audience falls below a set customer threshold.
Control group membership resets to zero on every send because small audiences cannot support any consistent group membership.
The control group may end up with zero members at low percentages on small audiences, so the percentage should move closer to 10 percent.

quiz.question: How does sending data through an orchestration differ from sending data through a campaign, based on how each one is set up?
options: An orchestration sends the results of a query or a database export to a destination, while a campaign sends the audience a segment defines.
An orchestration sends the audience defined by one or more segments, while a campaign sends the results of a Presto SQL query instead.
An orchestration and a campaign both require a segment as the starting audience, differing only in how sub-audiences get split apart.
An orchestration only supports paid media destinations, while a campaign only supports email and SMS destinations for its sub-audiences.

quiz.question: A marketer needs an audience to reach a Meta Ads Manager destination as quickly as possible after a campaign is scheduled. Based on typical destination timing described in Amperity's documentation, what should they expect?
options: Cloud storage destinations like Amazon S3 and paid media destinations like Meta Ads Manager both typically resolve within about 1 hour.
Paid media platforms like Meta Ads Manager typically take about 24-48 hours, longer than cloud storage or ESP destinations.
Email service providers like Klaviyo typically take longer than paid media platforms like Meta Ads Manager to receive an audience.
Meta Ads Manager and other paid media platforms typically resolve within 12-24 hours, the same window as most ESPs.

title: Designing Journeys
content: A journey is Amperity's automated, multi-step alternative to a campaign: instead of one send to one audience, a journey moves a defined audience through a sequence of decision points and actions -- sends, waits, and branches -- based on behavior and attributes, running on a recurring schedule rather than a single scheduled moment. This course covers how a journey's audience is scoped with inclusion, exclusion, exit, and goal conditions, the node types that make up a journey canvas, how journeys are measured over time, and how AmpAI can generate a working journey draft -- segment and canvas both -- from a plain-language description.

sections.heading: What Makes a Journey Different From a Campaign
sections.body:
The previous course in this track covered campaigns: a defined audience, split into sub-audiences, sent to destinations, on a one-time or periodically-refreshed schedule. A journey looks similar at a glance -- it also starts from a segment-defined audience and sends to destinations -- but its shape is fundamentally different. Amperity's documentation describes a journey as "an automated sequence for connecting with customers across channels like email, paid media, SMS, and direct mail," where each step is either a decision point or an action: send a message, wait for further engagement, or split the audience onto different paths.

The key distinction is time and structure. A campaign, even a recurring one, is still fundamentally a single send repeated on a cadence -- the same audience definition, refreshed and resent. A journey is a standing sequence: a customer who enters keeps moving through nodes over days, weeks, or months, potentially taking different paths depending on what they do along the way, until they either exit or reach the end of the canvas. Customers move through the sequence "based on criteria you specify, like customer behavior, attributes, or engagement history," and the path itself can branch, so two customers who enter the same journey on the same day can have entirely different experiences by the end of it depending on what they clicked, bought, or ignored.

Put concretely: a campaign answers "send this offer to this audience now (or on this repeating date)." A journey answers "whenever someone matches this profile, walk them through this sequence of messages and waits, adjusting course based on what they do." A win-back campaign sends one email to everyone currently dormant; a win-back journey enrolls a customer the moment they become dormant and keeps engaging with them -- an email, then a wait, then a different message depending on whether they opened it -- for as long as they stay in-journey.

sections.heading: Setting Up the Audience: Inclusion, Exclusion, Exit, and Goals
sections.body:
A journey's setup sidebar defines its audience the same way a campaign does, plus two mechanisms campaigns don't have. Inclusion segments determine which customers enter the journey at all -- one or more segments, unioned together. Exclusion segments remove specific customers from eligibility, the same use case as campaign exclusions: SMS opt-outs, email unsubscribes, anyone who shouldn't be enrolled regardless of otherwise matching.

Exit conditions are journey-specific: segments that, when a customer matches them, remove that customer from the journey outright, wherever they currently are in it. The documented example is a customer completing a purchase or opting out mid-journey -- someone doesn't need to keep receiving a win-back sequence once they've already come back and bought something. Up to ten exit segments can be configured, and like exclusions, they're unioned together -- a customer needs to match only one to exit.

Goal conditions look similar to exit conditions but behave differently: reaching a goal segment records that the customer hit a milestone, but does not remove them from the journey. Up to five goal segments are supported per journey, and they must be batch or SQL-based segments -- real-time segments aren't supported here. Finally, re-entry settings apply to recurring journeys: a customer who has already exited can re-enter later if they re-qualify against the inclusion criteria, which matters for something like a win-back journey where a customer could plausibly go dormant, come back, and go dormant again months later.

sections.heading: Nodes: The Building Blocks of a Journey Canvas
sections.body:
A journey is built visually on a canvas, starting from a Start node that displays and lets you edit the inclusion, exclusion, and foundational settings covered above. From there, journeys are assembled from a small set of node types that can be combined in any order. An Activate node sends a message to one or more configured destinations -- if different destinations in the same journey need different custom attributes attached, that requires separate Activate nodes rather than one node fanning out to all of them, and every node's name must be unique within its journey.

A Delay node pauses a customer's progression for a specified combination of days, weeks, or months before they move to the next step. The important, easy-to-miss detail here: "customers do not automatically move forward after the wait period ends. Progression only occurs the next time the journey runs." A journey doesn't evaluate delays continuously in real time -- it runs on a schedule (options include once, every 3 or 6 hours, twice daily, daily, weekly, monthly, or quarterly), and a customer whose delay technically elapsed at 2am on a journey scheduled to run daily at 9am simply waits until that 9am run to actually advance. Designing delay durations without accounting for the run cadence can silently add hours or days of unintended lag.

Branching happens through three more node types. A Conditional Split routes customers down different paths based on segment membership -- a matched path and an unmatched path. A Percent Split divides the audience by a randomly assigned percentage rather than by attribute, useful for A/B testing message variants; percentages across all paths from one split, including any control group, must total 100%, and control groups on a percent split default to 10%. An Individual Split creates distinct sub-audiences under custom conditions of their own. After any split, a Merge node -- which only appears as an option once a split exists -- can bring the separated paths back together into one continuing sequence.

sections.heading: Measuring a Journey: JTL, Milestones, and Percent-Split Testing
sections.body:
Because a journey runs continuously rather than firing once, measuring it requires more than a single send report. The Journey Travel Log (JTL) is the underlying record: it captures every stage transition a customer makes through the journey, along with metadata like timestamps, which branch of a split they took, and which exit segment (if any) removed them. It's the raw audit trail everything else in journey measurement is built from.

The Milestones Dashboard summarizes that raw data into something reviewable: goal achievements and exit events, aggregated across configurable time windows -- all-time, 7-day, 30-day, and 90-day. This is where the goal conditions defined during setup actually pay off -- without at least one goal segment configured, there's nothing for the Milestones Dashboard to report against beyond raw exits.

Percent-Split Testing is the most structured measurement tool: it compares goal achievement between the paths of a percent split, including any control-group path, and reports the incremental lift one path produced over another -- the actual point of holding out a control group in the first place. This measurement supports a maximum of two goal segments per split node, and like goal conditions generally, it requires batch segments; real-time segments aren't supported for this kind of measurement.

sections.heading: Drafting a Journey With AmpAI
sections.body:
The same Customer Data Assistant introduced in the Building Segments course extends to journeys, and the documentation is explicit that it produces both halves of a journey from one plain-language description: "a typical workflow might start with using the Customer Data Assistant to create a segment and journey, and then using the Manual edit option to open the specialized editors." This is the concrete difference from what a campaign-focused AmpAI request would produce: asking for a campaign audience yields a segment; asking for a journey yields both an entry segment and a populated multi-node canvas -- delays, splits, and Activate nodes assembled to match the description -- because a journey isn't a single send, it's the whole automated sequence covered earlier in this course.

The documentation's own test case makes this concrete: given the prompt "Create a win-back journey for churning platinum customers," the expected behavior is that the assistant "creates a segment using your churn + tier definitions, then creates the journey." That's two artifacts from one description -- an inclusion segment built from whatever churn and loyalty-tier attributes the tenant has, and a journey canvas wired to use it -- landing you at the Manual edit step with something substantive to review rather than a blank canvas.

The same limitation noted for segment generation applies here: a custom prompt "provides context but the Segment assistant and Journey assistant have their own specialized logic," meaning the generated journey should be treated as a strong first draft to validate against the JTL and Milestones Dashboard once it's running -- not as a finished, unreviewed sequence. The node-level judgment calls this course covered -- delay durations relative to run cadence, which segments belong on exit versus goal, how many percent-split paths a test actually needs -- are exactly the kind of detail worth checking in Manual edit before a generated journey goes live.

quiz.question: A journey includes a Delay node set to wait 3 days, and the journey's schedule is set to run once daily. According to Amperity's documentation, what happens to a customer once their 3-day wait period has elapsed?
options: The customer moves to the next node immediately and in real time, independent of the journey's run schedule.
The customer exits the journey automatically because delay periods that complete outside a scheduled run are dropped.
The customer does not move forward automatically; progression happens the next time the journey runs on its schedule.
The customer is moved to the next node only after an administrator manually approves the completed delay.

quiz.question: What is the key structural difference between a campaign and a journey, as described in Amperity's documentation?
options: A campaign runs continuously across many nodes while a journey only sends a single message to its audience one time.
A campaign and a journey are functionally identical, differing only in which page of the application each one gets configured on.
A campaign always requires an exit condition to be configured, while a journey never supports exit conditions at all.
A campaign sends a message or offer to an audience, while a journey is a multi-step sequence customers move through over time.

quiz.question: A journey is set up with a goal condition tracking "made a purchase." Per the documentation, what happens to a customer in the journey once they reach that goal segment?
options: The customer is not removed from the journey; reaching a goal segment only records that a milestone was achieved.
The customer is immediately removed from the journey, the same way that reaching an exit condition normally works for them.
The customer is moved into a Merge node regardless of which path they were on when the goal was reached.
The customer's control group assignment resets so they can be re-tested against the same goal segment again later.

title: From Use Case to Audience
content: Understanding attributes, operators, and AND/OR logic in the abstract is one thing; turning a real business goal into a working segment is another. This course walks through several of Amperity's documented worked examples -- finding dormant customers, isolating the top 20% of customers by revenue, and building a win-back audience -- as concrete segment logic, then closes by comparing the different kinds of attributes (boolean, relative-date, scored, categorical) that show up across these use cases so the pattern generalizes past these four specific examples.

sections.heading: Same Skill, Four Business Goals
sections.body:
Every worked example in Amperity's documentation follows the same shape, which should look familiar from the Building Segments course: open the Segment Editor with the customer 360 database selected, choose one or more attributes and operators that express the business goal as a condition, click Refresh to validate the resulting audience against segment insights, and Save As with a descriptive name. What changes case to case isn't the mechanics -- it's which attribute, from which table, with which operator, expresses a specific real-world definition like "dormant" or "top spender."

That's the actual skill this course is building: business stakeholders describe goals in plain language ("customers who've stopped buying," "our biggest spenders"), and translating that into a specific attribute and operator combination is a judgment call informed by what the data actually offers. Often there's more than one reasonable path to the same goal -- a raw date comparison versus a precomputed status field, for instance -- and picking between them is part of what the next few sections cover.

The four documented use cases referenced across this course are: identifying dormant customers, isolating the top 20% of customers by revenue, identifying early repeat purchasers, and building a win-back audience for lost customers. The next three sections walk through three of them as full worked examples; the final section folds in the fourth as a point of comparison.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Finding Dormant Customers
sections.body:
The business goal here is identifying customers who represent declining engagement and revenue potential -- concretely, people who haven't purchased in a defined window. Amperity's own default definition is precise: "a dormant customer is a customer who has not made a purchase within the previous 730 days" (two years).

The documented primary method builds this as a relative-date comparison: from the Transaction Attributes Extended table, add the Latest Order Datetime attribute, set the operator to "is after," enable the "Use relative dates" checkbox, and set the value to today minus 2 years. Read literally, that condition says "their most recent order happened before two years ago" -- which, phrased as "is after" a relative cutoff, is really excluding anyone whose latest order is more recent than the 730-day threshold, leaving only customers whose last purchase falls outside that window.

There's also a documented alternative that reaches the same audience through a different table entirely: the Historical Purchaser Lifecycle Status attribute from the Customer Attributes table, using "is in list" set to "Dormant." Instead of doing the date math yourself, this relies on a field Amperity has already precomputed into a lifecycle category. Both approaches are documented as valid; the raw-date version is transparent about exactly where the 730-day line sits and is easy to adjust to a different window, while the lifecycle-status version is faster to build and stays consistent with however "Dormant" is defined elsewhere in the tenant's reporting. As always, Refresh confirms the resulting count, past-year spend, and reachability before Save As names it something like "Dormant Customers."

sections.heading: Worked Example: Isolating the Top 20% by Revenue
sections.body:
This use case's business goal is two-sided: find which customers represent the top 20% of revenue generated in the past year, and see what share of total revenue that group actually accounts for -- a common way to check how concentrated a brand's revenue is among its best customers.

The documented segment logic uses the L12M Monetary attribute from the Transaction Attributes Extended table with the "is in list" operator, selecting values "9" and "10." Those values are RFM scores -- RFM stands for Recency, Frequency, Monetary, a common customer-scoring approach that ranks every customer into deciles (1 through 10) along each of those three dimensions separately. L12M Monetary is the monetary dimension scored specifically against the last 12 months: a customer scored 10 sits in the top decile of revenue generated over that period, and a customer scored 9 sits in the decile just below it. Selecting both 9 and 10 with "is in list" captures the top two deciles together, which is exactly the top 20% the business goal asked for -- the RFM scoring scheme and the percentile framing of the goal line up directly once you know deciles are involved.

Refreshing this segment surfaces the metrics the business goal actually needs: how many customers fall in the top 20%, what they spent in the past year in total, how many of them are still active, how many are eligible for future campaigns, and -- the second half of the original goal -- what percentage of total revenue this group represents. Save As with a name like "Top 20 Percent Customers During Previous Year" keeps the time window explicit in the segment name itself, since an L12M-scored segment's meaning shifts as the trailing 12-month window moves forward.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Winning Back Lost Customers
sections.body:
A win-back campaign is defined in the documentation as a series of personalized email messages sent to customers who've stopped engaging with a brand, aiming to get them to re-engage -- typically through incentives, product announcements, or personalized recommendations based on past purchases. Its success metric is the win-back percentage: the share of inactive customers who return to make a purchase within the measurement window.

Building the audience for this is where the AND logic from the Building Segments course shows up concretely, combining three separate conditions that all have to be true at once. First, Contactable Email from the Customer Attributes table, operator "is true" -- there's no point targeting someone with no usable email on file. Second, the documented recommendation adds Is Opted Into Email, also "is true" -- contactable is not the same as consented, a distinction this track has flagged before, and a win-back send is exactly the kind of campaign where skipping the opt-in check risks messaging someone who never agreed to receive marketing. Third, Days Since Latest Order from Transaction Attributes Extended, operator "is greater than or equal to," value 730 -- the same two-year inactivity threshold used to define dormancy, just expressed as a days-since count rather than a relative-date comparison against Latest Order Datetime.

Joined with AND, these three conditions narrow the audience to customers who are simultaneously contactable by email, opted in, and inactive for at least 730 days -- dropping any customer who fails even one of the three, which is precisely what AND is supposed to do. The documentation also notes two alternative single-attribute approaches that fold this logic into one precomputed field: Historical Purchaser Lifecycle Status set to "Dormant," or, for tenants with predictive modeling enabled, Predicted Customer Lifecycle Status set to "Lost." As with the dormant-customers example, the choice between building the AND condition explicitly and using a precomputed status attribute is a tradeoff between transparency and speed, not a right-versus-wrong decision.

sections.heading: Boolean, Relative-Date, Scored, and Categorical Attributes
sections.body:
Stepping back across the worked examples in this course, the attributes involved fall into a small number of recognizable shapes, and recognizing which shape you're dealing with speeds up building the next segment that doesn't happen to match a documented use case exactly.

Boolean attributes take a true/false value directly, no additional operator configuration needed beyond "is true" or "is false." The early repeat purchasers use case is the clean example: the Early Repeat Purchaser attribute from Transaction Attributes Extended, set to "is true," identifies customers matching Amperity's documented definition -- first-time buyers who returned to make a second purchase within 12 weeks, or 84 days, of their first. The documentation frames this specifically as a leading indicator for overall one-time-to-repeat-customer conversion, useful even though it doesn't capture every returning customer -- only the fast ones.

Relative-date attributes, like Latest Order Datetime in the dormant-customers example, compare a timestamp field against a dynamically shifting reference point ("today minus 2 years") rather than a fixed date, so the segment's membership stays current without manual updates. Scored attributes, like L12M Monetary in the top-20%-revenue example, express a customer's relative standing as a decile or similar rank rather than a raw dollar figure, which makes "is in list" against a small set of top scores a fast way to express a percentile cutoff. Categorical or picklist attributes, like Historical Purchaser Lifecycle Status, condense more complex underlying logic -- exactly the kind of AND-joined, multi-condition logic built explicitly in the win-back example -- into a single precomputed value you can filter on directly. None of these four shapes is inherently better than another; picking between a precomputed categorical field and building the underlying logic explicitly is the same tradeoff that came up twice in this course, between transparency into exactly what a segment counts and speed of building it.

quiz.question: Per Amperity's documentation, which condition defines the primary method for building a dormant customers segment?
options: Total Value of Orders from Unified Transactions is greater than zero within the previous 730 days of activity.
Latest Order Datetime from Transaction Attributes Extended is after a relative date of today minus 2 years.
Days Since Latest Order from Transaction Attributes Extended is less than or equal to 730 days since last purchase.
Historical Purchaser Lifecycle Status from Customer Attributes is in list and set specifically to the status Active.

quiz.question: In the "top 20% by revenue" use case, the segment uses the L12M Monetary attribute with the "is in list" operator set to values 9 and 10. What do these values represent?
options: Percentile rankings where 9 means the top 9% of spenders and 10 means the top 10% of spenders combined.
A count of the number of orders placed in the last 12 months, where 9 or 10 orders qualifies a customer.
RFM monetary scores, where higher deciles indicate customers with the highest revenue in the past year.
A loyalty tier level assigned to customers who have redeemed at least 9 or 10 reward certificates.

quiz.question: The win-back use case combines Contactable Email is true, Is Opted Into Email is true, and Days Since Latest Order >= 730 in a single segment. What does joining these three conditions with AND do to the resulting audience?
options: It returns customers who match any one of the three conditions alone, producing the broadest possible win-back audience.
It ignores the opt-in condition entirely, since AND only applies to numeric attributes like days since last order.
It returns every dormant customer regardless of contactability, since AND does not filter on boolean attributes at all.
It narrows the audience to only customers who satisfy all three conditions: contactable, opted in, and inactive 730-plus days.

title: How Sources Work
content: Amperity documents nearly 250 individual data sources, one page per third-party tool, but almost all of them configure the same underlying mechanism: a connection that pulls data into Amperity on a schedule. This course teaches that pattern directly, using SFTP as the simplest case, S3 and Fivetran as variations on the same pull, and Amperity Bridge as the exception that pulls and pushes data at once without ever copying it.

sections.heading: The Source Pattern: One Pull, Many Tools
sections.body:
Amperity's own documentation defines a source in one sentence: sources are "connections for Amperity to ingest data from other tools and platforms." That single definition covers close to 250 separate integration pages, from CRM systems and email platforms to cloud storage and data providers. Reading all 250 individually would mean re-learning the same handful of decisions again and again, because nearly every one of them is a variation on a single mechanism.

That mechanism is called a courier. A courier is the connection Amperity configures to actually pull data from a source on your behalf: it holds the hostname, credentials, file path or table name, and everything else needed to reach into the origin system and bring data back. Setting up almost any source follows the same two-phase shape: first you gather the connection details for the tool you're connecting to, then you configure the courier itself and tell it which files or tables to load.

Once a courier can see data, Amperity still needs to know what to do with it on arrival, and that's where load strategy comes in. Upsert updates any record that already exists and inserts any record that's new, leaving everything else untouched. Truncate and upsert instead deletes every existing record in the target before loading, which is the right choice when the source always hands over a complete snapshot rather than only what changed since last time.

Finally, couriers can run once, manually, or be added to a courier group that runs on a recurring schedule, so the same pull repeats automatically at whatever cadence the business needs. Get details, configure the courier, choose a load strategy, set a schedule -- that four-step shape is what every one of the roughly 250 source pages is really describing, just with different nouns.

sections.heading: SFTP: The Baseline Pull
sections.body:
SFTP is the simplest version of the pattern above, which makes it a useful baseline before looking at anything more elaborate. Setting one up means gathering a hostname and port, a username and passphrase (or a private key, if that credential type is selected), an optional host public key for validating the SSH connection, and optionally a PGP key if the files arriving from the remote server are encrypted.

Data has to live in a specific remote folder, and Amperity is strict about how that folder is written: the path must start with a forward slash, for example /folder/name. From there, files can be chosen by browsing the folder directly or by giving a filename pattern that matches files loaded on a recurring basis, so a new file dropped in that folder tonight gets picked up by tomorrow's scheduled pull without anyone touching the configuration again. Amperity infers the file's delimiter, compression, escape character, quote character, and whether a header row is present, all from a sample file provided during setup.

Everything else follows the general pattern from the previous section exactly: the courier is configured with those connection details, a load strategy of upsert or truncate-and-upsert is chosen depending on whether the remote files are deltas or full snapshots, and the courier either runs manually or joins a courier group on a schedule. SFTP doesn't introduce any new concept -- it's the pattern with the fewest moving parts.

sections.heading: S3 and Fivetran: Same Pattern, Different Plumbing
sections.body:
Amazon S3 follows the identical shape but swaps out authentication. Rather than a username and passphrase, Amperity uses cross-account role assumption: the customer creates an IAM role inside their own AWS account that grants Amperity temporary, revocable permission to read a specific bucket, instead of ever handing Amperity a long-lived credential. That means the customer keeps direct control of the IAM policy, can manage files in the bucket without going through Amperity, and can revoke access at any time without contacting Amperity at all. Amperity's documentation calls S3 "the most often used data source across all Amperity tenants," and describes its typical uses as one-time file uploads, recurring uploads from systems that lack a direct connector, and Parquet exports from cloud databases.

Fivetran adds a genuine wrinkle, but it's a wrinkle in plumbing, not in pattern. Fivetran itself is "a third-party application that collects data from a wide variety of sources, and then loads that data to Snowflake tables." When a company already uses Fivetran to centralize data in Snowflake, or wants access to a source Amperity doesn't natively support, Amperity doesn't connect to the original system at all -- it connects to Snowflake, using its own built-in connector to read the tables Fivetran already populated there. That's a two-hop pull instead of a one-hop pull: Fivetran moves data from the original tool into Snowflake, and a separate Amperity courier then moves it from Snowflake into Amperity.

Even with that extra hop, the direction of travel is unchanged. SFTP, S3, and Fivetran all end the same way: data flows into Amperity's customer database, and nothing flows back out through that same connection. That's true of the overwhelming majority of the roughly 250 sources documented. Bridge is the one that breaks it.

sections.heading: Bridge: When Pull Becomes Two-Way
sections.body:
Amperity Bridge is described in its own documentation as allowing users to "share data between Amperity and a data lakehouse using industry-standard data formats," and it supports three platforms: Databricks (using a protocol called OpenSharing), Google BigQuery, and Snowflake. The bidirectional claim isn't just marketing language -- the setup itself requires customers to "configure inbound and outbound shares in Amperity" for whichever platform they connect, meaning the same integration can move data from the lakehouse into Amperity and from Amperity back out to the lakehouse, rather than only one direction like every source discussed so far.

The other thing that separates Bridge from a courier is that it doesn't copy anything. SFTP and S3 couriers physically move files into Amperity's own storage before loading them. Bridge instead grants access to data where it already lives: for Databricks, "OpenSharing generates temporary credentials that allow access to individual data files in cloud storage without copying data," and for Snowflake, the same idea is called secure data sharing, enabling "bi-directional data access between Amperity and Snowflake without copying data." Amperity's documentation refers to this as a zero-copy approach -- access to a shared table is controlled without ever replicating the underlying rows.

The practical effect is live data: because nothing is duplicated, a change made to the source table in the lakehouse is visible to Amperity without waiting for a scheduled courier to run again, which matters most for very large tables that would be expensive to copy on every load.

sections.heading: Picking a Pull Strategy for the Data You Have
sections.body:
Put together, the four examples in this course cover almost every decision the other roughly 245 source pages ask you to make. If data lives in files on a server you control, that's SFTP or a similar file-based courier. If data already lives in cloud storage, that's an S3-style source authenticated through cross-account role assumption rather than a shared credential. If another tool is already centralizing your data in a warehouse like Snowflake, that's a Fivetran-style two-hop source reading from that warehouse instead of the original system. And if you need live, two-directional access to a lakehouse without ever copying its data, that's Bridge.

None of those four decisions changes when the tool's name changes. A source page for a CRM platform or an email platform is still choosing between the same authentication styles, the same one-hop-versus-two-hop question, the same upsert-versus-truncate-and-upsert load strategy, and the same manual-versus-scheduled courier group. Once those four choices are familiar, reading any individual source's documentation is mostly confirming which values apply to that specific tool, not learning a new mechanism.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the general pattern behind how Amperity sources bring data in?
options: Amperity continuously scans every connected tool's API and imports new records automatically, without ever once needing connection details from the customer.
Data is pushed out from Amperity to each third-party tool nightly, and the receiving tool alone decides which of those records it will accept.
Amperity is given connection details for a tool, a courier pulls data on a schedule using upsert or truncate-and-upsert, landing results in the database.
Every source stages its files in Amazon S3 first, and Amperity then reads only from S3, regardless of where the data originally came from.

quiz.question: A source sends a complete, full snapshot of every record each time it runs, rather than only the records that changed. Which load strategy fits, and why?
options: Truncate and upsert, because it clears existing records before loading so the destination matches the latest snapshot, not stale rows.
Upsert, because it always inserts new rows first and only updates duplicate rows afterward, which is exactly how a full snapshot must be handled.
Truncate and upsert, because it removes only the specific rows that were deleted from the source file, which is what a snapshot requires.
Upsert, because it deletes the entire destination table before loading, ensuring snapshot data is never duplicated anywhere inside Amperity.

quiz.question: According to Amperity's documentation, what actually distinguishes Bridge from sources like SFTP, S3, or Fivetran?
options: Bridge only supports Databricks as a platform, while SFTP, S3, and Fivetran can each connect to any cloud data warehouse a customer uses.
Bridge copies files into Amperity's own storage before they can be used, whereas SFTP and S3 read data directly without ever copying it.
Bridge only moves data out of Amperity toward an external destination, while SFTP, S3, and Fivetran only ever move data into Amperity.
Bridge configures inbound and outbound shares and reads data directly without copying it, while the others only pull data into Amperity.

title: How Campaigns & Destinations Work
content: Sending data out of Amperity follows two mechanisms, not one: orchestrations that deliver a query's results directly to a destination, and campaigns that build a segment, split it into treatment groups, and send that audience out on a schedule with a validation step first. This course grounds both mechanisms in three representative destinations -- Klaviyo and Braze for marketing automation, and Meta Ads Manager for advertising -- rather than surveying the full list of destination integrations.

sections.heading: The Send Pattern: Two Mechanisms, Not One
sections.body:
Amperity's documentation for the Klaviyo destination lists three distinct ways data can reach it: orchestrations sending query results, orchestrations or campaigns sending audiences, and orchestrations or campaigns sending events. Underneath that list are really only two mechanisms, and the difference between them matters more than which specific destination is on the receiving end.

An orchestration is the simpler of the two: it runs a query against Amperity's data and sends the result set directly to a destination, on a schedule if needed. There's no audience-building step in between -- the query defines exactly which rows go out, and the destination receives them.

A campaign is built for a different job: sending a segment -- a saved set of customer records selected by shared criteria -- out as an audience. A campaign splits that segment into treatment groups, which are subsets of the audience that can each be pointed at a different destination, message, or experiment condition, and only then sends the resulting audience to one or more destinations on a configured schedule. Campaigns are the mechanism behind audience and event sends; orchestrations are the mechanism behind plain query-result sends.

sections.heading: Klaviyo: Profiles, Locations, and Everything Else
sections.body:
Klaviyo is described in Amperity's documentation as "an email platform for targeting, personalizing, measuring, and optimizing email and Facebook campaigns." Amperity sends data to it through Klaviyo's REST API, specifically its Update Profile endpoint, using either an API key or OAuth to authenticate.

What actually gets sent is shaped by column names. Named profile fields like email, first_name, last_name, external_id, phone_number, organization, title, and image map to Klaviyo's own profile schema. Address-related columns are grouped into a nested location object. Everything else -- any column that isn't a recognized profile or location field -- is automatically bundled into a properties object, so a custom column added on the Amperity side shows up in Klaviyo without any extra mapping step.

One detail matters more than it looks: email is the field Klaviyo uses to generate a unique customer identifier for each profile. That makes the email column do double duty -- it's both a piece of profile data and the key Klaviyo uses to decide whether an incoming record matches an existing customer or creates a new one, which is why setup requires explicitly designating email as the audience's primary key.

sections.heading: Braze: Attributes, Not Duplicate Records
sections.body:
Braze's own documentation describes it as "a marketing automation platform that uses customer profile attributes and segments to build custom experiences, and then map those experiences to campaigns." Where Klaviyo organizes incoming data into profile, location, and properties objects, Braze organizes it into two attribute categories: profile attributes, which describe who a customer is (names, birthdates, email addresses, phone numbers), and custom attributes, which describe how that customer has interacted with the brand (purchase history, loyalty status, value tier).

Braze attaches this data to existing customer profiles rather than creating new ones, and it does so efficiently: the integration "only sends list membership and attribute that have changed since the previous update," so a scheduled sync doesn't resend a customer's entire attribute set every time, only what's actually different.

Braze also enforces a constraint that's easy to trip over: its API requires exactly one identifier type per request, chosen from external_id, braze_id, or user_alias. A request that mixes identifier types for the same record isn't merged or reconciled -- it's rejected outright, which is why setup requires picking one identifier type up front rather than leaving it flexible per record.

sections.heading: Meta Ads Manager: Campaigns Built for Audiences
sections.body:
Meta Ads Manager is where the campaign mechanism from the first section shows up in its fullest form, because advertising audiences have no equivalent to an orchestration's simple query-result send. The workflow starts with the Segment Editor, where a segment is built from any attribute in the customer database, and continues by adding that segment to a campaign, selecting Meta Ads Manager as the destination for at least one treatment group, and configuring a schedule.

Before the real audience goes anywhere, Amperity's documentation is explicit about validating first: send a sample audience with a very small membership to Meta Ads Manager and confirm it looks correct there before sending the full audience. Only after that check does the full audience get sent, with up to 24 hours allowed before it's available inside Meta Ads Manager for building ads.

Meta Ads Manager also exposes a choice that Klaviyo and Braze don't: which underlying table the audience is built from, Merged Customers or Unified Paid Media, trading off Amperity's "best profile" per customer against a fuller multi-record view. That's a targeting decision specific to advertising audiences, not something a query-result orchestration to an email platform ever has to make.

sections.heading: Matching the Send Mechanism to the Job
sections.body:
Across all three destinations, the mechanism tracks the job, not the vendor. Klaviyo and Braze both primarily receive profile and attribute updates -- data about who a customer is and what they've done -- which fits an orchestration's query-result send or a straightforward campaign audience just as well. Meta Ads Manager only receives audiences, never a raw query result, because an advertising platform has nothing to do with a plain list of rows; it needs a segment, split into treatment groups, validated with a sample before the real send goes out.

That's the pattern worth carrying into any other destination this course didn't cover: ask whether the job is delivering the current state of a set of records (orchestration) or delivering a built, tested audience for a campaign to act on (campaign), and the right mechanism follows from the answer -- regardless of which of the many destination pages you end up reading.

quiz.question: Klaviyo's documentation lists orchestrations sending query results separately from orchestrations or campaigns sending audiences and events. What's the practical difference between an orchestration and a campaign here?
options: An orchestration is always a one-time manual export, while a campaign always runs automatically on a schedule with no manual trigger ever available at all.
An orchestration runs a query and sends results directly to a destination, while a campaign builds a segment into treatment groups and sends an audience.
An orchestration can only send data to advertising platforms, while a campaign can only ever send data to email and SMS platforms instead.
An orchestration sends data only after a campaign has already delivered the same audience, acting as a confirmation step before the real send.

quiz.question: What constraint does Braze's API enforce on identifiers, and why does it matter for how Amperity sends data?
options: Every request must include all three identifier types together, or Braze cannot match the record to an existing customer profile.
Braze requires Amperity to generate a brand-new identifier for every record, since it never accepts identifiers created outside its own system.
Braze accepts any identifier type as long as the values are capitalized consistently, since matching is case-sensitive rather than type-specific.
Braze's API accepts exactly one identifier type per request, so mixing external_id and braze_id for the same record gets the request rejected.

quiz.question: Before sending a full audience from a segment to Meta Ads Manager, what does Amperity's documentation recommend?
options: Send a sample audience with a very small membership first and confirm it looks correct in Meta Ads Manager before sending the full audience.
Send the full audience immediately, then rely on Meta Ads Manager's built-in preview mode to check its accuracy after delivery instead of before.
Skip validation for audiences built from the Unified Paid Media table, since Amperity has already pre-validated that table.
Wait 24 hours after creating the segment before sending anything, since Meta Ads Manager requires a cooling-off period on new audiences.

title: Choosing the Right Integration
content: Amperity groups its connector documentation into a handful of categories -- CRM & Marketing Automation, Email & SMS, Advertising Platforms, Data Platforms & Cloud Storage, and Analytics & BI -- and the category tells you more about what an integration is for than any individual vendor's name does. This course is a decision guide: given a job to do, which category to reach for, using the source and destination mechanics from the first two courses in this track as the reasoning underneath each answer.

sections.heading: Start With the Job, Not the Tool
sections.body:
The two prior courses in this track established two mechanisms worth remembering here. On the way in, sources pull data through a courier, either directly (SFTP, S3) or through an extra hop (Fivetran), or bidirectionally without copying anything at all (Bridge). On the way out, orchestrations send a query's results directly to a destination, while campaigns build a segment into treatment groups and send it as a validated audience. Every category below is really just a grouping of tools that lean on one or both of those mechanisms for a particular kind of job.

That's a more useful lens than memorizing which of the roughly 250 documented integrations does what. A team that knows it needs to trigger a message, build an ad audience, or centralize raw data doesn't need to know Klaviyo from Braze or S3 from Fivetran up front -- they need to know which category of tool does that kind of job, and then the specific vendor's documentation fills in the details from a pattern they already understand.

sections.heading: "I want to trigger email or SMS sends"
sections.body:
This job points at Email & SMS -- the category Klaviyo and Braze both belong to, covered in the previous course. These platforms are built to receive profile and attribute data about customers (who they are, what they've done) and use it to trigger or personalize messages, which is why Klaviyo maps incoming columns into profile, location, and properties objects and Braze maps them into profile and custom attributes.

Whether the send goes out as a campaign audience or an orchestration's query result depends on what's actually needed. A one-off list of customers who match a query -- everyone who bought a specific product last month, say -- fits an orchestration. A recurring, segmented send with multiple treatment groups, like a win-back flow tested against a control group, fits a campaign. Either way, the destination category is the same; only the sending mechanism changes.

sections.heading: "I want to build ad audiences"
sections.body:
This job points at Advertising Platforms -- the category Meta Ads Manager belongs to. Unlike Email & SMS destinations, advertising platforms have no orchestration path at all: there's no such thing as sending a plain query result to a Facebook or Instagram ad campaign. Every send is a campaign, because every send is an audience -- a segment split into treatment groups and validated with a small sample before the real send goes out.

Expect this category to also ask a targeting question the others don't: which underlying customer table the audience is built from. Meta Ads Manager's choice between Merged Customers and Unified Paid Media -- trading a single best profile per customer against a fuller multi-record view -- is representative of the kind of decision Advertising Platforms integrations tend to expose, because ad audiences are judged on reach and precision in a way a marketing email list usually isn't.

sections.heading: "I want to centralize raw data or connect a warehouse I already use"
sections.body:
This job points at Data Platforms & Cloud Storage, the category SFTP, S3, Fivetran, and Bridge all belong to. If the data starts as files sitting somewhere -- a vendor's SFTP drop, an S3 bucket, an export from another internal system -- a direct courier-based source is the fit, authenticated either by credentials (SFTP) or cross-account role assumption (S3). If another tool is already centralizing that data into a warehouse like Snowflake, a two-hop source reading from that warehouse is the fit instead of trying to connect to the original system directly.

If the actual requirement is different -- live, two-directional access to a lakehouse without ever duplicating its data -- that's not a source in the pull sense at all; it's Bridge, still filed under Data Platforms & Cloud Storage but solving a different problem than every other integration in that category. The category groups these together because they're all about where data lives and how Amperity reaches it, not because they all work the same way underneath.

sections.heading: CRM & Marketing Automation and Analytics & BI: The Other Two Categories
sections.body:
Two categories remain. CRM & Marketing Automation sits close to Email & SMS but usually functions as a source as often as a destination -- a CRM is frequently where customer records originate, not just where messages get sent, so integrations in this category tend to support both directions of the pattern rather than committing to one. Analytics & BI, by contrast, is almost always on the receiving end: these integrations exist to receive query results and aggregated data for reporting and analysis, which makes them a near-pure fit for the orchestration mechanism from the previous course rather than the campaign mechanism.

The reasoning holds together across all five categories: name the job first -- trigger a message, build an ad audience, centralize files, connect a CRM, or feed a reporting tool -- and the category, and the mechanism underneath it, follow from that job. The vendor is the last detail to fill in, not the first.

quiz.question: A team wants to send a triggered email when a customer abandons a cart, following the pattern of Email & SMS platforms like Klaviyo and Braze. Which mechanism fits, and why?
options: A source, because a triggered send requires Amperity to first pull historical email engagement data in before any message can go back out.
A Bridge integration, because only a bidirectional, zero-copy connection can support a real-time triggered message reaching a customer directly and instantly.
A campaign, because campaigns are built for sending segment-based audiences and events to destinations like Klaviyo or Braze, fitting a triggered send.
A courier, because couriers are the mechanism Amperity uses to schedule outbound communication to any connected third-party platform.

quiz.question: A team wants to build a lookalike audience for a paid social campaign. Which category fits, and what should they expect to configure?
options: Data Platforms & Cloud Storage, because advertising audiences must be staged as raw files in a warehouse before any ad platform can accept them.
Advertising Platforms, because these integrations send segment-based audiences through a campaign, validated with a small sample first.
Analytics & BI, because advertising platforms mainly consume aggregated reporting data rather than individual customer-level audiences.
CRM & Marketing Automation, because advertising audiences are just customer records sent through the same orchestration used for email sends.

quiz.question: A company already centralizes customer data in Snowflake and wants Amperity to both read from and write back to those tables without duplicating data. Which category are they describing, and which mechanism does it point to?
options: Analytics & BI, because BI tools are the only integrations in Amperity that support two-way data movement with a connected warehouse.
CRM & Marketing Automation, because the platforms in that category are supposedly built directly on top of Snowflake by default.
Email & SMS, because Snowflake commonly acts as a staging layer for messages before they ever reach a destination like Klaviyo.
Data Platforms & Cloud Storage, pointing to a bidirectional, zero-copy connection like Bridge rather than a one-directional pull.
